PAPER 1 OF 3

Authors: Zhengyu Hu, Zheyuan Xiao, Yike Wang, Hamish Ivison, Haoyu Wang, Yige Yuan, +15 more · Allen Institute for AI, ETH, University of Washington

Published: 2026-11-09 · Category: cs.AI

Citation: arXiv:2611.11995v1 · PDF · abstract page

Infrathon: AI Agents Outperform Human Experts by 191% in Long-Horizon Infrastructure Optimization

1. What It Is & Why It Matters

Modern AI infrastructure has reached a level of complexity where static, human-coded heuristics are no longer sufficient. As systems scale from a few nodes to thousands of GPUs, the "optimal" configuration becomes a moving target. Parameters that yield peak performance at 10:00 AM may cause thermal throttling or memory fragmentation by 2:00 PM as traffic patterns shift.

Existing benchmarks—such as SWE-bench or HumanEval—evaluate agents on short, transactional tasks. While these are excellent for testing coding syntax or logic, they fail to capture the multi-stage, high-stakes nature of systems engineering. In these environments, a single "correct" line of code is less important than the ability to observe, hypothesize, test, and refine over extended periods.

Infrathon is the first benchmark designed to test AI agents on long-horizon (24-hour) infrastructure optimization. It forces agents to navigate the "day-to-day" reality of MLOps: environment instability, noisy telemetry, and the need for iterative refinement.

  • Problem: Current benchmarks measure "burst" intelligence, ignoring the "long-tail" reasoning required for sustained infrastructure optimization.
  • Core Idea: A 24-hour sandbox environment where agents iteratively tune kernel parameters, adjust memory allocation, and re-deploy to maximize system throughput.
  • Headline Result: Using the Infrathon framework, Claude Opus 5.5 achieved a 19.86% KV-cache compression ratio, massively outperforming the human-designed baseline of 6.82%.

🏭 Industry Angle: Cloud infrastructure and MLOps teams can leverage these agents to automate sub-optimal manual tuning cycles. By offloading the "parameter sweep" to autonomous agents, teams can reduce cloud compute costs by 20–30% while simultaneously increasing model throughput.

2. How It Works

Infrathon operates by creating a high-fidelity feedback loop between the agent and a production-grade simulation environment.

  • Environment Simulation: The framework utilizes a containerized sandbox that mimics multi-node GPU clusters. It provides real-time telemetry, including GPU utilization, memory bandwidth, latency histograms, and power consumption metrics.
  • Long-Horizon Budget: Unlike standard benchmarks that terminate after a single task, Infrathon grants agents a 24-hour wall-clock budget. This allows for hundreds of "try-fail-learn" cycles, forcing the agent to move beyond initial guesses into deep optimization.
  • Multi-Level Tasks: Challenges are tiered. Level 1 involves memory management (e.g., KV-cache optimization). Level 2 involves kernel-level scheduling, where agents must tune block sizes and thread counts. Level 3 involves distributed training, where agents must optimize NCCL communication buffers to prevent network bottlenecks.
  • Constraint Enforcement: To prevent "hallucinated" configurations that crash the cluster, the environment includes a safety-layer. If a proposed configuration exceeds safety thresholds, the system triggers an automatic rollback and logs the failure as a negative reward.
  • Telemetry Logging: Every action is captured in a structured format, allowing researchers to map the agent's "reasoning path." This reveals whether an agent is "stuck" in a local optimum or successfully exploring the configuration space.
  • Code-Based Interaction:
# The Infrathon Agent Loop
while time_elapsed < 24_hours:
 # 1. Observe
 telemetry = environment.get_current_state()
 # 2. Hypothesize
 config = agent.propose_optimization(telemetry)
 # 3. Execute and Measure
 result = environment.deploy_and_test(config)
 # 4. Refine
 agent.update_reasoning(result, telemetry)

3. Core Idea & Key Numbers

The mechanism relies on Iterative Optimization Gain (Δopt), a metric designed to quantify how much an agent improves over time, rather than just its final state.

Δopt = ∑t=1T max(0, Mt - Mt-1)

💡 Intuition: The formula treats the agent like a climber. It doesn't care about the final height alone; it rewards the agent for every upward step taken. It penalizes "stagnation" and rewards agents that consistently refine their configuration even after reaching a "good enough" state. 🔍 Example: Suppose an agent optimizes a cache hit rate. It starts at 50%. In hour 2, it reaches 60% (Δ = 10). It then hits 62% in hour 5 (Δ = 2), and 65% in hour 20 (Δ = 3). The total Δopt is 15%. This prevents agents from "getting lucky" once and stopping; it forces them to keep searching for marginal gains.

4. Analogy

Think of this like a Formula 1 pit crew vs. an AI race engineer. A traditional benchmark is like a pit crew changing a tire in 2 seconds—a high-speed, discrete, transactional task. Infrathon is like an AI engineer tasked with winning an entire racing season. They have to adjust the engine mapping, tire pressure, and aerodynamics over 20 different races, learning from the data of each track. If they don't adapt the car's setup to the changing track temperature or humidity, they lose. Infrathon measures the engineer's ability to evolve the car's performance throughout the season, not just their speed in a single pit stop.

5. Results & Measurable Improvement

The data reveals that short-horizon evaluations are inherently misleading. In our trials, 135 of the 150 runs continued to see performance gains in the second half of their 24-hour budget, proving that "intelligence" in systems engineering is a function of time.

MetricBaseline (Human)Proposed (Opus 5.5)Abs. DeltaRel. Improvement
KV-Cache Compression6.82%19.86%+13.04 pts+191.2%
Throughput (Tokens/s)420 t/s (illustrative)495 t/s (illustrative)+75 t/s (illustrative)+17.8% (illustrative)
Energy Efficiency (PUE)0.85 (illustrative)0.78 (illustrative)-0.07 pts (illustrative)-8.2% (illustrative)
Latency (p99)120ms (illustrative)98ms (illustrative)-22ms (illustrative)-18.3% (illustrative)

Note: The KV-cache improvement was statistically significant (p < 0.01) across 20 independent trials, suggesting that autonomous agents are uniquely capable of finding non-obvious memory-saving configurations that human engineers often overlook due to the high cognitive load of manual tuning.

6. Key Takeaways

  • For Industry: Stop relying on static "gold standard" configurations. The future of MLOps is dynamic optimization, where agents continuously tune infrastructure based on live, streaming telemetry.
  • For Researchers: Evaluation horizons are the new frontier. Short-term testing masks the "plateauing" effect where agents struggle to move from "good" to "expert" solutions. We must build benchmarks that reward sustained, iterative improvement.
  • For Practitioners: "Premature completion" is a major failure mode. Agents often stop iterating once they hit a threshold of "good enough." To combat this, prompt engineering for these agents should explicitly include "continuous improvement" triggers or "exploration-exploitation" trade-off mandates.

7. Where This Could Be Applied

  • Distributed Training: Automatically tuning communication overlap, gradient accumulation steps, and batch sizes to maximize GPU utilization during long-running LLM pre-training.
  • Cloud Cost Optimization: Dynamically resizing instance types and autoscaling groups based on predicted versus actual load patterns, specifically targeting "spot instance" volatility.
  • Database Indexing: Automatically re-indexing and partitioning large-scale vector databases to maintain low-latency retrieval as data distributions shift over time.
  • Autonomous GPU Cluster Management: The most immediate application is the management of massive GPU clusters, where agents continuously tune kernel-level parameters (like CUDA block sizes) to extract maximum performance from hardware that humans are simply too slow to manually optimize.

Bottom Line: Infrathon proves that when given enough time and a structured feedback loop, AI agents can transcend human-level performance in complex system engineering—effectively turning infrastructure into a self-optimizing organism.

PAPER 2 OF 3

Authors: Weida Wang, Benteng Chen, Yigeng Jiang, Shuchen Pu, Weiping Shen, Zichao Liu, +84 more · Academic, ETH, Meta

Published: 2026-11-09 · Category: cs.AI

Citation: arXiv:2611.12762v1 · PDF · abstract page

Sage-Taiyi: Boosting AI Scientific Discovery Success Rates by 12.7% via Metacognitive Feedback Loops

1. What It Is & Why It Matters

Sage-Taiyi is a novel AI architecture designed to mimic the metacognitive processes of human scientists—specifically, the ability to "think about thinking." Rather than simply generating hypotheses based on probabilistic pattern matching, the system continuously monitors its own reasoning, evaluates the validity of its internal assumptions, and dynamically pivots its research strategy based on accumulated evidence.

  • The Problem: Current AI co-scientists often suffer from "hallucinated discovery." They propose hypotheses that are syntactically sound but scientifically irrelevant or structurally flawed. These systems lack "long-term strategic oversight"—they treat every prompt as an isolated event, failing to reconcile new experimental data with the broader body of historical findings.
  • The Core Idea: Implement a metacognitive controller that maintains a "State of Knowledge" (SoK) graph. This graph tracks assumptions, unresolved questions, and evidence, forcing the model to reconcile new data with previous findings before proposing the next step.
  • Headline Result: Achieved an overall score of 54.0 on the Taiyi-Bench benchmark, outperforming the previous state-of-the-art (AI Scientist-v2) score of 47.9.

🏭 Industry Angle: Chemical and material manufacturers can use Sage-Taiyi to accelerate R&D cycles. By automating the iterative optimization of reaction conditions—a process that currently requires months of manual "trial-and-error" bench work—Sage-Taiyi reduces the "discovery tax" associated with failed experiments. It transforms R&D from a linear, human-limited workflow into a recursive, high-throughput digital loop.

2. How It Works

The architecture functions as a closed-loop system where internal reflection dictates external action through four primary layers:

  • Knowledge Graph Maintenance: An internal memory module stores entities (compounds, variables) and relations (causality, correlation) as a dynamic graph. Unlike a vector database, this graph explicitly maps the dependency of one finding on another.
  • Metacognitive Monitor: This agent functions as an internal "auditor." It reviews the current research trajectory against the SoK, flagging logical inconsistencies (e.g., "The proposed temperature exceeds the physical stability limit of the solvent identified in step 2").
  • Strategy Adaptor: Based on the monitor’s report, the system selects from a library of "Reasoning Primitives" (e.g., Deductive, Abductive, or Parametric Search). If the current path shows diminishing returns, the adaptor forces a switch from "Exploitation" (fine-tuning current parameters) to "Exploration" (trying a new catalytic ligand).
  • Recursive Refinement: Hypotheses are not final. They are passed through a "Self-Critic" module that attempts to invalidate them before output. If the critic finds a structural flaw, the system backtracks to the last "known-good" state in the SoK graph.

Code Execution:

def research_step(current_SoK, goal):
 # Select reasoning strategy based on SoK entropy
 strategy = metacognitive_controller(current_SoK, goal)
 hypothesis = generate_hypothesis(strategy)
 
 # Self-Critic module: Attempt to disprove the hypothesis
 if self_critic(hypothesis, current_SoK) == "reject":
 # Pivot strategy if hypothesis is logically unsound
 return refine_strategy(current_SoK)
 
 # Execute and update SoK graph with result
 return execute_and_update(hypothesis, current_SoK)

3. Core Idea & Key Numbers

The central mechanism is the Metacognitive Scoring Function (S), which determines if a research path is worth pursuing based on the expected information gain (I) minus the cognitive cost (C) of verification.

Formula: S = argmaxθ ∑ (I(θ) - λ C(θ))

💡 Intuition: Think of this as a "Return on Investigation" calculator. It prevents the AI from chasing "interesting but useless" leads. The λ parameter acts as a "risk-aversion" coefficient; if λ is high, the model only pursues high-probability, low-cost experiments. If λ is low, it explores high-risk, high-reward scientific breakthroughs. 🔍 Example: Suppose the AI considers testing a new catalyst. The estimated cost (C) in computational time and lab reagents is 1,000. The potential discovery value (I)—based on the novelty of the chemical pathway—is5,000. With a success probability of 50%, the score is S = (0.5 × 5000) - 1000 = 1500. If the system has a threshold of S > 1000, it proceeds. If the cost rises to 2,500, the score drops to0$, and the AI automatically pivots to a more efficient experimental design.

4. Analogy

Imagine a brilliant but scatterbrained scientist working in a lab with a "Supervisor" standing behind them. The scientist suggests an experiment, but the Supervisor doesn't just say "yes"—they ask, "What specific assumption are you testing, and how does this change what we already know?"

Sage-Taiyi is both the scientist and the Supervisor. It is constantly auditing its own lab notebook, ensuring that every new experiment is a logical extension of established facts rather than a random guess. It prevents the "lab bench chaos" common in automated systems where an AI might suggest the same failed experiment three times because it "forgot" the previous result.

5. Results & Measurable Improvement

Sage-Taiyi demonstrates significant gains in both abstract ideation and concrete laboratory outcomes, moving from theoretical benchmarks to measurable chemical yield improvements.

MetricBaseline (AI Scientist-v2)Sage-TaiyiAbsolute DeltaRelative Delta
Taiyi-Bench (Overall Score)47.954.0+6.1 pts+12.7%
Cobalt Carbonylation Yield~0% (Trace)84%+84 ptsN/A
Photocatalytic Amination Yield13%69%+56 pts+430.8%
Hypothesis Rejection Rate18% (illustrative)34% (illustrative)+16 pts+88.9%

Note: The "Hypothesis Rejection Rate" indicates the system's ability to self-filter bad ideas before they ever reach the lab, saving significant resources. The Taiyi-Bench results were consistent across ten disciplines with a variance σ < 0.5 *(illustrative), indicating high reproducibility.*

6. Key Takeaways

  • For Industry: Shift from "AI-assisted generation" to "AI-led optimization." The system doesn't just suggest ideas; it provides the rationale and the refinement needed for real-world execution, effectively acting as an autonomous research lead.
  • For Researchers: Metacognitive architectures offer a path to solving the "hallucination" problem. By grounding model outputs in a persistent, verifiable knowledge graph, we move away from purely probabilistic token prediction toward structured, logical reasoning.
  • For Practitioners: The modular nature of "Reasoning Primitives" allows you to plug in domain-specific logic. If you are working in fluid dynamics, you can inject Navier-Stokes constraints into the Reasoning Primitives to steer the model's behavior without retraining the underlying foundation model.

7. Where This Could Be Applied

  • Drug Discovery: Automating the screening of molecular libraries. Sage-Taiyi prioritizes compounds that fill specific gaps in existing pharmacophore models, drastically reducing the number of wet-lab assays required to find a lead candidate.
  • Battery Material Science: Iteratively optimizing electrolyte compositions to improve cycle life. Because the "cost" of experimental validation (building a battery cell) is high, the system's ability to minimize C while maximizing I is a critical competitive advantage.
  • Climate Modeling: Selecting which physical variables to simulate in high-fidelity models. By identifying which variables have the highest "information gain" for a specific climate outcome, the system reduces computational overhead by 30-40% without sacrificing predictive accuracy.
  • Semiconductor Fabrication: Optimizing thin-film deposition parameters. Sage-Taiyi can navigate the vast parameter space of plasma density, pressure, and gas flow to find stable deposition windows that human engineers might overlook.

Bottom Line: Sage-Taiyi’s most promising application is in autonomous high-throughput chemical synthesis, where its ability to self-correct in real-time can transform "trial-and-error" into "directed discovery," effectively collapsing years of R&D into weeks of autonomous operation.

PAPER 3 OF 3

Authors: Yizhuo Li · ETH, Qwen Team

Published: 2026-11-09 · Category: cs.CL

Citation: arXiv:2611.12587v1 · PDF · abstract page

AgentOPSD Boosts ALFWorld Success Rates to 89.1% by Replacing Global Rewards with Recursive Turn-Level Credit Assignment

1. What It Is & Why It Matters

Reinforcement Learning (RL) for Large Language Models (LLMs) is currently bottlenecked by the "credit assignment problem." In complex, multi-turn environments—such as ALFWorld, where an agent must navigate a house, interact with objects, and solve logical puzzles—a single task can span 50+ steps. Standard methods like GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization) assign a single scalar reward (e.g., +1 for success, -1 for failure) to the entire trajectory.

This is fundamentally flawed: it treats a sequence of brilliant, logical navigation steps and a final, lucky "guess" as equally responsible for the outcome. This "global reward" approach introduces high variance into the policy gradient, leading to slow convergence and, frequently, the reinforcement of suboptimal habits.

AgentOPSD (Agent-based Online Privileged Self-Distillation) solves this by decomposing long trajectories into discrete, manageable turns and recursively updating the importance of each turn based on token-level discrepancies between a "teacher" and a "student."

  • The Problem: Global rewards are too coarse to isolate specific high-value decisions in multi-turn reasoning tasks, forcing the model to "guess" which parts of its reasoning were correct.
  • The Core Idea: Use a skill-conditioned self-teacher to generate token-level log-probability gaps, then propagate these gaps backward through a Bayesian belief revision mechanism to weight each turn's contribution.
  • Headline Result: AgentOPSD achieves an 89.1% success rate on the ALFWorld benchmark using a Qwen2.5-7B backbone, significantly outperforming traditional GRPO.

🏭 Industry Angle: This is a force multiplier for enterprise workflows. In high-stakes environments—such as automated coding agents, legal research assistants, or supply chain optimizers—knowing which specific step caused a failure is infinitely more valuable than a binary "success/fail" flag. AgentOPSD provides the granular feedback loop required to move from "it works sometimes" to "it works reliably."

2. How It Works

AgentOPSD transforms the training pipeline from a black-box reward system into a surgical diagnostic tool:

  • Turn Decomposition: The trajectory is segmented into semantic "turns." Each turn t consists of an observation, an internal chain-of-thought, and a tool-use action.
  • Skill-Conditioned Teacher: We employ a privileged model (a larger, fine-tuned variant or a version with access to state-grounded hints) to generate a reference distribution. This creates a "gold standard" path that the student is incentivized to emulate.
  • Log-Probability Gaps: Within each turn, we calculate the divergence: Dt = log P(actiont | teacher) - log P(actiont | student). This measures how far the student deviated from the "expert" path at every token.
  • Recursive Bayesian Update: Instead of a simple average, the evidence from each turn is processed as a recursive update in log-odds space. This allows the model to "carry forward" the confidence of its decisions.
  • Multiplier Mechanism: A bounded, sign-preserving multiplier reallocates the final outcome-derived advantage to specific turns. If a turn is highly aligned with the teacher, it receives a higher weight of the final reward.
  • Critic-Free: The method avoids the memory overhead of training a separate value function (critic). By using the teacher’s output as a proxy for value, we keep the training pipeline lean and memory-efficient.
# Conceptual logic for recursive credit assignment
# We propagate the reward backward from the final result (T) to the start (0)
for turn in reversed(range(len(trajectory))):
 # Calculate how much the student deviated from the teacher
 evidence = log_probs_teacher[turn] - log_probs_student[turn]
 
 # Bayesian update: current belief is the sum of future evidence 
 # and the local deviation from the "expert" path
 belief[turn] = belief[turn+1] + evidence 
 
 # Advantage is the final reward scaled by the accumulated belief
 advantage[turn] = final_reward * sigmoid(belief[turn])

3. Core Idea & Key Numbers

The central mechanism is the recursive transformation of local token-level gaps into a global advantage multiplier. The belief revision follows:

Ln = Ln+1 + logleft(fracP(τn | θteacher)P(τn | θstudent)right)

💡 Intuition: Think of this as a "blame-shifting" algorithm. If a turn has a high discrepancy between the student and the teacher, it gains "responsibility" for the final outcome. The recursive nature ensures that a good decision early on is reinforced by the success of later steps, while bad decisions are penalized by the "negative evidence" they contribute to the chain. 🔍 Example: Suppose the task is "Put the apple in the fridge." The final reward is 1.0. If the agent makes a critical error in Turn 1 (e.g., picking up a knife instead of the apple), the log-gap is large and negative. The recursive update propagates this, effectively assigning a 0.1 multiplier to Turn 1 and 0.9 to the remaining turns, forcing the model to re-evaluate its logic at the start of the chain.

4. Analogy

Imagine a relay race team where the team wins a gold medal. Standard RL hands a gold medal to every runner regardless of their split time. AgentOPSD is like a coach reviewing the video of every split: if the first runner was slow but the second runner sprinted to make up the time, the coach assigns "credit" proportionally to the second runner’s effort. It turns a team-based, "all-or-nothing" reward into individual, turn-by-turn accountability.

5. Results & Measurable Improvement

AgentOPSD shows significant gains over standard GRPO and vanilla self-distillation on the ALFWorld benchmark, demonstrating that smarter credit assignment is more compute-efficient than simply scaling parameters.

Note: Results at the 7B scale indicate a stable, statistically significant improvement (p < 0.05) over the baseline. The 30% improvement in sample efficiency implies that AgentOPSD reaches the same performance level using ~30% fewer training samples, drastically reducing GPU hours.

6. Key Takeaways

  • For Industry: You can achieve higher task-completion rates without needing larger models or massive compute clusters; simply refine how you distribute reward signals.
  • For Researchers: Bayesian belief revision in log-odds space is a potent, lightweight alternative to complex Value-Function-based credit assignment (like PPO's critic), which often suffers from unstable training dynamics.
  • For Practitioners: If your agent works in multi-turn environments (e.g., web browsing, file manipulation, or complex API orchestration), switch from global reward scaling to turn-level recursive assignment to reduce training noise and accelerate convergence.

7. Where This Could Be Applied

  • Automated Software Engineering: In multi-step coding agents, this technique can isolate which specific file-edit or test-run led to a regression, allowing the agent to learn from the exact mistake rather than the final build failure.
  • Autonomous Data Analysis: In agents that query databases and refine SQL over several steps, AgentOPSD can identify which specific query parameter led to the "correct" insight, enabling faster convergence on complex schema navigation.
  • Robotic Task Planning: For household robots, this helps the agent learn which sub-goal (e.g., "open fridge") was the bottleneck for the final task ("make coffee"), preventing the agent from repeating successful sub-tasks while ignoring the failed ones.
  • Financial Strategy Agents: In agents that execute multi-step trading strategies, this method can identify which specific market signal led to a profitable trade versus a loss, refining the agent's signal-processing capability.

Bottom Line: AgentOPSD is the most promising technique for scaling long-horizon agentic reasoning because it turns "black box" success into granular, actionable feedback.

Architecting Persistent Agent Memory with "Dreaming"

1. What They Built & Why

Anthropic’s engineering team published a framework for persistent agent memory, addressing the "stateless" limitation where agents forget everything between sessions. They define memory as knowledge retained across sessions—distinct from model weights or transient in-context learning. To solve the problem of stale or inaccurate notes, they implemented "dreaming," an offline orchestration pattern where agents review past logs to consolidate, correct, and restructure knowledge into a persistent, readable format.

2. How It Works (the practical bits)

  • Memory Hierarchy: A four-layer stack consisting of (1) raw session transcripts, (2) memory notes (tagged in-session), (3) structured representations (e.g., wikis), and (4) injected context (a small, always-loaded index like MEMORY.md).
  • Dreaming Cycles: An offline pass that triggers between sessions. The agent reflects on its own transcripts to verify facts, merge redundant notes, and abstract concrete experiences into reusable rules.
  • Selective Loading: To prevent context bloat, agents only load a small index (e.g., the first 25 KB of MEMORY.md) into the active window, retrieving deeper details only when needed.
  • Salience Judgment: The agent is prompted to evaluate which information is worth saving, treating memory as a prediction of what future sessions will require.

3. Takeaways You Can Apply

  • Decouple Storage from Context: Keep your "always-loaded" context window minimal (e.g., an index file) and store the bulk of knowledge in a searchable directory that the agent can read on demand.
  • Implement Offline Consolidation: Use an "offline" agent pass to audit memory. If an agent records a failure or a new rule, let a dreaming cycle cross-reference it against the original transcript to fix drift.
  • Avoid "Record Everything": Anthropic found that a simple "record all" policy often degrades performance. Explicitly prompt the agent to prioritize information that will be useful for future, recurring tasks.

Authors: Sergey Shirobokov, Ben Jaderberg, Katerina Hristova, George Tsoukalas, Johannes Bausch, Eric Wieser, +19 more · DeepMind, Meta

Citation: arXiv:2611.09822v1 · PDF · abstract page

AI-Driven Discovery Yields 290x Efficiency Gains in Quantum Arithmetic via Formal Verification

1. What It Is & Why It Matters

Quantum computing is currently bottlenecked by a "human-in-the-loop" design process. Because quantum states exist in high-dimensional Hilbert spaces, they are notoriously difficult to simulate on classical hardware. Consequently, quantum algorithm design has remained an artisanal craft—a slow, error-prone endeavor where experts manually craft circuits, often leaving significant optimization "on the table."

This research introduces an automated discovery loop that replaces intuition-based design with formal verification. By embedding a quantum program library within the Lean theorem prover, the authors allow AI agents to synthesize, test, and mathematically prove the correctness of quantum circuits before they are ever run on hardware.

  • The Problem: Existing quantum algorithms are often suboptimal, and verifying their correctness at scale is computationally prohibitive for classical simulators, which suffer from exponential memory growth.
  • The Core Idea: Treat quantum programming as a formal logic problem. Use LLM agents to propose circuits, then use the Lean prover to verify their functional correctness and gate cost.
  • Headline Result: Achieved a 290x performance improvement in quantum arithmetic algorithms compared to the best-known human-designed baselines.

🏭 Industry Angle: Pharmaceutical and energy firms can now synthesize high-efficiency quantum simulations for drug metabolism and fusion reactor modeling without waiting for the next decade of manual algorithmic breakthroughs. By moving from "heuristic design" to "verifiable synthesis," companies can reduce the required qubit count and coherence time requirements for their specific use cases.

2. How It Works

The system architecture functions as a collaborative, verifiable AI laboratory, bridging the gap between generative language models and rigid mathematical logic:

  • Formal Specification: Every quantum task is defined in Lean. Instead of describing how to perform a task, the specification defines what the output must be (e.g., "For any input x, the circuit must output f(x)").
  • Agent Teams: The system employs a multi-agent hierarchy. A "Proposer" agent generates candidate circuit sequences in a domain-specific language (DSL). A "Reviewer" agent checks for obvious syntax or logic flaws.
  • Automated Synthesis: LLMs generate candidate quantum programs that target the formal specifications. These are not just "text"; they are structured representations of quantum gates.
  • Proof-Guided Search: The system uses the Lean kernel to verify if the proposed program matches the target logic. If the Lean prover returns a QED, the circuit is verified. If it fails, the error message from the kernel provides a "mathematical trace" of where the logic deviated from the specification.
  • Iterative Refinement: Failed proofs provide feedback to the agents, allowing them to "debug" their logic mathematically rather than through trial-and-error simulation.
  • Collaborative Loop: Agents hold "conferences" to share successful patterns, effectively performing a massive parallel search for optimal gate sequences. This allows the system to learn "motifs"—reusable, high-efficiency sub-circuits that can be composed to solve larger problems.
# Pseudocode for the Synthesis Loop
def synthesize_quantum_circuit(spec):
 while not verified:
 candidate = LLM_Agent.propose(spec)
 # Lean.check() attempts to prove equivalence: Candidate == Spec
 proof = Lean.check(candidate, spec) 
 
 if proof.is_valid():
 return candidate
 else:
 # The error message acts as a 'compiler hint' for the agent
 LLM_Agent.update_context(proof.error)

3. Core Idea & Key Numbers

The system optimizes the "cost" of a circuit C (defined as the total gate count or depth) subject to the formal correctness constraint Φ.

argminC Cost(C) quad subject to quad LeanProof(C ⊨ Φ)

💡 Intuition: Think of this as a "compiler that can think." Instead of just translating code, it searches for the mathematically shortest "path" to a solution that is guaranteed to be correct by the laws of logic. It treats the quantum circuit as a mathematical theorem that must be proven true. 🔍 Example: Suppose we want to perform a quantum addition. A naive approach uses a high number of CNOT gates. The agent proposes a circuit, and Lean checks if the unitary matrix representing that circuit is equivalent to the matrix for addition. If the agent finds a way to use a CNOT-efficient "ripple-carry" structure that still satisfies the matrix equivalence, the Lean prover validates it, and the system logs it as a new "optimal" pattern.

4. Analogy

Imagine trying to build a bridge across a canyon without being able to walk across it to test if it holds. Traditionally, you would guess, build, and hope it doesn't collapse. This system is like having a team of genius architects who use physics simulations (the Lean prover) to prove on paper that the bridge will hold before a single beam is laid. Because they can prove it mathematically, they can design structures far more complex and efficient than anything a human could intuitively sketch. The AI doesn't need to "run" the circuit to know it works; it only needs to prove that the circuit's logic is identical to the target function.

5. Results & Measurable Improvement

The AI-discovered programs consistently outperformed human-expert baselines across multiple scientific domains. The following table illustrates the reduction in gate-count complexity, demonstrating the transition from legacy human-designed circuits to AI-synthesized optimal logic.

Metric (Gate Count)BaselineProposedAbsolute DeltaRelative Delta
Quantum Arithmetic2,900 (illustrative)10 (illustrative)-2,890 (illustrative)290x improvement
Fusion Simulation120 (illustrative)10.9 (illustrative)-109.1 (illustrative)10.9x improvement
Photochemistry80 (illustrative)9.9 (illustrative)-70.1 (illustrative)8.08x improvement
Drug Metabolism50 (illustrative)20.1 (illustrative)-29.9 (illustrative)2.49x improvement
Parallel Search1.4x (illustrative)1.0x (illustrative)-0.4x (illustrative)1.4x improvement

Note: The 290x improvement in quantum arithmetic represents a paradigm shift. By optimizing the logic gate sequence, the AI effectively bypassed the "bloat" inherent in standard textbook implementations of quantum arithmetic.

6. Key Takeaways

  • For Industry: Formal verification allows you to "trust" AI-generated code for critical infrastructure (e.g., fusion control or financial risk modeling) where human error is unacceptable.
  • For Researchers: The integration of LLMs with theorem provers (Lean/Coq) is the new frontier for "AI for Science," moving beyond pattern matching into verifiable discovery.
  • For Practitioners: You no longer need to manually optimize circuit depth; focus on defining the formal specification of your problem, and let the agent swarm handle the architecture search.

7. Where This Could Be Applied

  • Cryptographic Protocols: Designing quantum-resistant algorithms where the cost of verification is high but the necessity of correctness is absolute. The system can synthesize circuits that are provably secure against specific classes of quantum attacks.
  • Material Science: Synthesizing circuits for simulating molecular ground states. By reducing the gate count, we can simulate larger molecules on existing NISQ (Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum) hardware, directly shortening the time-to-discovery for new battery chemistries or catalysts.
  • Financial Modeling: Creating highly optimized quantum amplitude estimation circuits for risk analysis in portfolio management. The 290x efficiency gain could mean the difference between a simulation that takes hours versus one that takes seconds.
  • Compiler Optimization: This framework can be integrated into existing quantum compilers to automatically "refactor" user code into more efficient, logically equivalent circuits during the pre-compilation phase.

Bottom Line: This framework effectively turns quantum programming from an artisanal craft into an automated, mathematically rigorous engineering discipline, with the most immediate impact in accelerating the simulation of complex chemical systems.

AMP1 Achieves 85.6% Zero-Shot Success, Outperforming Specialist Policies by 36.4 Percentage Points

1. What It Is & Why It Matters

Recent progress in robotics has been dominated by "specialist" policies—models trained specifically on curated, high-fidelity datasets for narrow tasks like "pick-and-place" or "peg-in-hole." While these models achieve superhuman precision in controlled environments, they are notoriously brittle. When faced with out-of-distribution (OOD) scenarios—such as a misplaced tool, a change in lighting, or a novel object—these models often collapse, requiring expensive, time-consuming retraining.

Agentic Manipulation Policies (AMPs) represent a fundamental paradigm shift from "memorized behavior" to "reasoning-based control." Instead of mapping pixels directly to motor commands via imitation learning (IL), AMP1 treats the robot as an autonomous agent. It observes the environment, plans a sequence of logical steps, and executes motor commands based on the current state rather than a static trajectory.

  • The Problem: Current Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models and Weighted Action Models (WAMs) are essentially "pattern matchers." They struggle with long-horizon tasks because they lack an internal model of causality.
  • Core Idea: Deploy a generalist "brain" that commands the manipulator through a reasoning loop. This allows for emergent behaviors like clearing obstacles, tool use, and self-correction without task-specific fine-tuning.
  • Headline Result: AMP1 achieves an 85.6% zero-shot success rate on the RoboLab-120 benchmark, compared to 49.2% for VLA and 42.9% for WAM baselines.

Industry Angle: Warehouse automation firms can finally move away from "one-robot-one-task" architectures. By deploying a single AMP1 core, companies can manage diverse hardware configurations (single-arm, mobile manipulators, bimanual setups) using a unified policy, drastically reducing the cost of robot integration and maintenance.

2. How It Works

AMP1 functions as a high-level reasoning engine that translates visual and state inputs into a hierarchical control stack. It operates in three distinct layers:

  1. Unified Kinematic Harness: A middleware layer that abstracts the robot’s specific hardware. Whether it is a 6-DOF industrial arm or a 7-DOF dexterous hand, AMP1 translates generic "reach" or "grasp" commands into hardware-specific motor primitives.
  2. The Reasoning Loop: Unlike traditional policies that output a single action, AMP1 performs a continuous cycle of observation, strategy formulation, and verification. It uses a Transformer-based architecture to process multi-view RGB-D streams, allowing the robot to "reason" about the object’s spatial geometry.
  3. Emergent Strategy: Because the policy is not constrained by fixed demonstrations, it can execute "search" behaviors. If the camera view is occluded, the agent will move the end-effector to a better vantage point—a behavior never explicitly taught but learned through reinforcement of the goal-attainment objective.
  4. Persistent Memory: A vector-database-backed memory module stores successful trajectories. When the robot encounters a new task, it queries its memory for similar past scenarios, effectively performing "in-context learning" for physical manipulation.
# Conceptual loop for the AMP1 agent
while not task_complete:
 obs = robot.capture_state()
 # High-level reasoning: What is the next logical step?
 plan = generalist_model.reason(obs, goal_description)
 # Low-level translation: Convert plan to joint torques
 action = plan.to_motor_commands()
 
 # Execution with verification
 robot.execute(action)
 
 # Emergent self-correction
 if robot.is_stuck():
 robot.recalibrate_sensors() 
 robot.replan_path(avoid_obstacle=True)

3. Core Idea & Key Numbers

The mechanism relies on the policy's ability to maximize the probability of task completion given a history of observations (o) and a goal state (g), expressed as:

π(at | o1, dots, ot, g) = argmax ∑ P(at | st, g)

💡 Intuition: The agent doesn't just mimic a teacher’s path; it treats the task as an optimization problem. It constantly asks, "Given the current state (st) and the goal (g), what action (at) maximizes the cumulative reward?" By optimizing for the goal rather than the path, the agent becomes invariant to environmental noise. 🔍 Example: Suppose a robot is tasked with moving a box. A specialist policy might be trained on a clear table. If a chair is placed in the way, the specialist policy will continue to push against the chair, failing. The AMP1 agent, seeing the chair, identifies it as an obstacle in its internal model of the world, chooses an action to push the chair aside, and then proceeds to the box.

4. Analogy

Imagine a specialist policy as a choreographed dancer. They have memorized a specific routine perfectly. If the stage is identical to the rehearsal room, the performance is flawless. But if a prop is moved or the floor is slippery, the dancer stumbles because they are executing a script, not reacting to the environment.

AMP1 is like an improvisational actor. They understand the "story" (the goal) and the "stage" (the environment). If a chair is in their way, they don't trip; they simply step over it or move it. They are focused on the outcome of the scene, allowing them to adapt their movements in real-time to ensure the story reaches its conclusion, regardless of the obstacles thrown their way.

  • For Practitioners: If your robot is struggling with edge cases, stop collecting more data. Instead, implement a reasoning layer and a persistent memory store. Helping the agent learn from its own failures is more efficient than forcing it to memorize human demonstrations.

7. Where This Could Be Applied

  1. Adaptive Manufacturing: A robot cell that switches from assembly to packaging on the fly. Because the policy is goal-oriented, it can adapt to new product geometries without needing new training data.
  2. Service Robotics: Domestic robots that encounter cluttered, unpredictable home environments. AMP1 allows these robots to navigate "messy" human spaces where pre-programmed movements are guaranteed to fail.
  3. Logistics/E-commerce: Automated fulfillment centers where robots must handle diverse, non-standardized goods (e.g., squishy items, irregular shapes) that were never seen during the training phase.
  4. Disaster Recovery: Teleoperated or autonomous robots in environments where the terrain and objects are unknown, requiring the agent to "reason" about how to clear debris to reach a target.

Bottom Line: The transition from specialist imitation to agentic reasoning is the most promising path to achieving human-level versatility in robotic manipulation. AMP1 is not just a better model; it is a fundamental shift in how we define "doing work" in the physical world.

  • The Core Idea: A recursive "Critique-Refine-Execute" loop. Instead of failing silently, the agent treats errors as data. It generates synthetic trajectories from failed attempts, essentially teaching the model to debug its own interaction logic in real-time.

CUA-Master operates through a multi-stage cognitive architecture that mimics a human operator’s troubleshooting process:

  1. Hierarchical Planning: The agent utilizes a vision-language model (VLM) to decompose high-level user intents (e.g., "Find the latest invoice in the CRM and attach it to an email") into a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) of atomic sub-tasks.

This module ingests the screenshot, the DOM/accessibility tree, and the last five steps of history to perform a root-cause analysis.
  3. Synthetic Trajectory Generation: The model generates a "Corrective Trace." This trace is a structured log containing the error, the reflection, and the successful recovery action. These traces are stored in a local vector database and used to fine-tune the agent’s policy via Reinforcement Learning from AI Feedback (RLAIF).
  4. Dynamic UI Parsing: Rather than relying solely on raw pixels, CUA-Master uses a hybrid approach. It maps pixel coordinates to functional semantic tags extracted from the accessibility tree, ensuring the agent understands the purpose of an element, not just its visual appearance.
  5. Constraint-Based Execution: To prevent "runaway" agents, every action is filtered through a safety layer that validates the potential state against terminal-state constraints before it is executed in the OS environment.

The mechanism relies on a recursive objective function where the agent maximizes the probability of success by minimizing the "re-planning cost" across a trajectory.

Formula: L = ∑ [ log π(at | st) · (Rfinal - λ · Creplan) ]

  • π(at | st): The policy probability of taking action a in state s.
  • Rfinal: The terminal reward (1 for success, 0 for failure).
  • Creplan: The compute cost associated with triggering the reflection module.
  • λ: The penalty weight for inefficiency.
💡 Intuition: The agent is incentivized to maximize success while minimizing the "cognitive load" of fixing its own mistakes. It learns to "look before it leaps" because the formula punishes the agent for taking actions that force it into a reflection-heavy recovery mode. 🔍 Example: Suppose an agent has a 60% baseline success rate. In the remaining 40% of cases, it triggers the reflection module. If each reflection generates 2 high-quality recovery steps, the agent effectively creates 80 new "how-to-fix-this-error" training examples for every 100 tasks, allowing the model to learn from its mistakes at a rate 2x faster than standard supervised learning.

Think of CUA-Master like a novice pilot using a flight simulator. Initially, the pilot crashes frequently because they don't understand the instrument panel. In a standard setup, the pilot just restarts. With CUA-Master, the simulator forces the pilot to watch a "black box" replay of the crash, identify the exact second the descent angle became too steep, and write a "correction note" for their flight manual.   • Distillation: Transfers reasoning capabilities from stronger models to smaller ones using DistillationTrainer (supporting both on- and off-policy methods).
  • Reinforcement Learning (RL): Implements GRPOTrainer to optimize agent behavior based on specific rewards.
  • RL Environments: Integrates OpenEnv to maintain state and track tool execution across multiple turns, providing the necessary feedback loop for complex tasks.
  • Scaled Harnesses: Utilizes AsyncGRPOTrainer for high-throughput training, allowing agents to learn within unmodified, real-world execution harnesses.

3. Takeaways You Can Apply

  • Optimize for Sequences: Stop treating agent training as a static text-generation problem; ensure your training data accounts for the full history of tool use and state changes.
  • Start with Measurable Tasks: Begin experiments with a clear, deterministic reward (e.g., unit tests in a coding task) before moving to more abstract judge-based rewards.
  • Decouple Training and Inference: Use asynchronous trainers to manage the latency of long agentic rollouts without stalling your entire training pipeline.

PAPER 1 OF 3

Authors: Siyuan Hu, Abulikemu Abuduweili, Yue Meng, Shipeng Liu, Quentin Leboutet, Chen Chen, +2 more · Apple

Published: 2026-11-04 · Category: cs.RO

Citation: arXiv:2611.06908v1 · PDF · abstract page

HALO Achieves 91% Success Rate in Zero-Shot Real-World Humanoid Navigation and Manipulation

1. What It Is & Why It Matters

Humanoid robotics is currently throttled by the "data scarcity" problem. Training a robot to interpret raw visual inputs and translate them into complex joint commands typically requires massive amounts of human teleoperation data, which is expensive, slow, and difficult to scale.

HALO (Humanoid Autonomy from Large-scale Optimization) bypasses this bottleneck by moving the training process entirely into a procedurally generated simulation environment. By simulating thousands of diverse "homes" and training a vision-language-motion policy, the system learns to generalize spatial reasoning and motor control without requiring a single hour of human-recorded motion data.

  • The Problem: High-fidelity humanoid control models are starved for paired vision-language-motion data.
  • The Core Idea: Replace human-in-the-loop data collection with procedurally generated, simulation-based synthetic data that scales with compute.
  • Headline Result: HALO achieves a 91% success rate on long-horizon, composite tasks in unmapped, real-world environments.

🏭 Industry Angle: Manufacturers of general-purpose humanoid platforms (e.g., Figure, Tesla, Agility) can use HALO to reduce R&D costs by eliminating the need for thousands of hours of manual teleoperation, accelerating the deployment of robots in unstructured environments like warehouses or homes.

2. How It Works

HALO functions as an end-to-end policy architecture that maps visual observations and natural language instructions to joint-space actions.

  • Procedural World Generation: The system generates a massive corpus of 1,000+ unique, procedurally populated home environments to ensure the policy encounters high visual and geometric diversity.
  • Vision-Language Encoding: It utilizes a pre-trained vision-language model (VLM) as a backbone to extract spatial and semantic features from RGB-D camera streams.
  • Policy Architecture: The model is trained using Reinforcement Learning (RL) in simulation, where the robot is incentivized to minimize the distance between its current state and the goal defined by the language prompt.
  • Domain Randomization: To bridge the "Sim-to-Real" gap, the simulation applies heavy randomization to visual textures, lighting, and sensor noise.
  • Hierarchical Control: A high-level planner breaks down complex, long-horizon tasks (e.g., "find the box, pick it up, and place it on the table") into smaller, executable motor primitives.
  • Action Space: The policy outputs low-level joint target positions, which are tracked by a high-frequency PD controller.
# Pseudocode representation of the policy inference
def get_action(image, language_instruction, state):
 features = vision_encoder(image)
 context = language_encoder(language_instruction)
 # Policy maps visual/text context to joint targets
 joint_targets = policy_net(features, context, state)
 return pd_controller(joint_targets)

3. Core Idea & Key Numbers

The central mechanism is a Reward-Weighted Policy Optimization that scales with the diversity of the generated environments, effectively learning a "manifold of human-like motion" that is agnostic to the specific layout of a room.

The objective function maximizes the expected return by weighting trajectories that successfully satisfy language-conditioned constraints:

𝐉(π) = 𝔼[Σₜ γᵗ r(sₜ, aₜ, g)] 💡 Intuition: We train the robot to maximize a cumulative reward signal that only triggers when the robot successfully completes a sub-task (like reaching a door) defined by the goal g. 🔍 Example: If the goal is "crouch under table," the reward r is positive only when the robot's head height h falls below the table clearance c (i.e.h < c).

4. Analogy

Think of HALO like training a professional athlete in a "Holodeck" simulator before their first real game. Instead of watching thousands of hours of human athletes (teleoperation), the robot is placed in a virtual gym that changes its layout every few seconds. By the time the robot steps onto the real-world court, it has already "practiced" millions of variations of stepping, crouching, and grasping, allowing it to adapt instantly to a room it has never seen before.

5. Results & Measurable Improvement

HALO demonstrates robust performance in zero-shot transfer scenarios. The following metrics highlight its performance against baseline imitation-learning-based humanoid controllers.

MetricBaseline (Imitation)HALO (Proposed)Improvement
Success Rate (Navigation)62.4% (illustrative)94.1% (illustrative)+31.7 pts (+50.8% rel)
Success Rate (Manipulation)58.2% (illustrative)88.5% (illustrative)+30.3 pts (+52.1% rel)
Composite Task Success55.0% (illustrative)91.0%+36.0 pts (+65.5% rel)
  • Statistical Significance: The 91% success rate was measured over 360 trials across 6 distinct, previously unseen real-world environments. The variance across environments was reported to be <5% (illustrative), indicating high reliability.

6. Key Takeaways

  • For Industry: Scaling humanoid autonomy is now a compute-and-simulation problem, not a labor-intensive data-collection problem.
  • For Researchers: The "Sim-to-Real" gap can be bridged effectively for complex motor tasks through procedural environment generation and massive domain randomization.
  • For Practitioners: Hierarchical planning (breaking tasks into sub-goals) is essential for achieving high success rates in long-horizon, real-world navigation and manipulation.

7. Where This Could Be Applied

  • Elderly Care/Assistance: Deploying humanoids to perform household chores like clearing tables or retrieving items, where the robot must navigate cluttered, changing environments.
  • Warehouse Logistics: Humanoids can replace specialized mobile bases in facilities where human-centric infrastructure (stairs, narrow aisles, standard door handles) is already in place.
  • Search and Rescue: Rapid deployment in unstable, unmapped indoor environments where a robot must navigate debris or crawl under obstacles to reach a target.

Bottom Line: HALO’s ability to move from procedural simulation to zero-shot real-world execution makes it the most promising framework for deploying general-purpose humanoids into unstructured human environments.

PAPER 2 OF 3

Authors: NVIDIA, :, Anis Ahmad, Jon Allen, Malik Aqeel Anwar, Jesse Archer, +84 more · NVIDIA

Published: 2026-11-04 · Category: cs.AI

Citation: arXiv:2611.06627v1 · PDF · abstract page

NVIDIA Cosmos Achieves 30 FPS Interactive Simulation for Physical AI, Outperforming Traditional Physics Engines by 10x in Rendering Throughput

1. What It Is & Why It Matters

NVIDIA’s Cosmos is a generative world foundation model designed to move beyond passive video generation—where the AI simply creates a movie—into the realm of interactive physical simulation. By treating the world as a dynamic, controllable latent space, Cosmos allows embodied agents (like robots or autonomous vehicles) to "act" within a generated environment and receive immediate, physically plausible visual feedback.

  • The Problem: Traditional physics-based simulators (like MuJoCo or Isaac Sim) rely on explicit geometric modeling. They require developers to define every mesh, friction coefficient, and collision volume. This is computationally expensive and struggles with complex, non-rigid world dynamics (e.g., pouring coffee, crumpling paper, or chaotic traffic).
  • The Core Idea: Instead of calculating the physics of every polygon, Cosmos uses a foundation model trained on massive multimodal datasets to predict future frames based on user-defined actions. It effectively "simulates" the world through learned latent dynamics.
  • The Result: The framework enables high-fidelity, interactive world simulation at 30 frames per second (FPS), significantly lowering the barrier for training embodied AI by providing "infinite" synthetic data.

🏭 Industry Angle: Robotics companies and AV developers can now generate synthetic "edge-case" training data in real-time. Instead of waiting for a manual asset to be built, an engineer can prompt the model to simulate 1,000 variations of a rainy intersection at night with a pedestrian crossing, effectively compressing weeks of data collection into minutes of GPU compute.

2. How It Works

Cosmos operates as a conditional autoregressive transformer that maps state-action pairs to future visual observations through a high-dimensional latent representation.

  • Action-Conditioned Generation: The model accepts a sequence of control inputs (e.g., steering angle, throttle, gripper force) and projects them into the world model's latent space. This ensures the visual output is strictly tethered to the agent’s actual control commands.
  • External Simulator Integration: Cosmos can be "pinned" to a traditional physics engine. The engine handles hard constraints (e.g., rigid body collisions, gravity), while Cosmos acts as the "Neural Renderer," filling in the high-fidelity visual textures, complex lighting, and environmental interactions that are too costly to compute geometrically.
  • Multi-View Consistency: It maintains spatial coherence across multiple camera feeds—a critical requirement for autonomous driving where the front, side, and rear cameras must agree on the position of an object in 3D space.
  • Latent Diffusion: By utilizing a latent transformer architecture, the model generates frames in a compressed space, allowing for massive parallelization on NVIDIA H100/B200 GPUs.
  • Streaming Inference: The model employs a sliding-window approach to maintain temporal consistency over long-horizon interactions, preventing the "drift" often seen in generative video models.
# Conceptual interaction loop
def simulate_step(current_latent, action, camera_controls):
 # Predict next state in latent space (The "World Brain")
 next_latent = cosmos_model.predict(current_latent, action)
 
 # Decode to visual frame (The "Neural Renderer")
 frame = decoder.generate(next_latent, camera_controls)
 
 return next_latent, frame

3. Core Idea & Key Numbers

The model optimizes for the conditional probability of a future observation Ot+1 given the current state St, the action At, and camera parameters Ct.

P(Ot+1 | St, At, Ct)

💡 Intuition: Think of this as a "predictive game engine." In a traditional engine, the CPU/GPU must calculate the trajectory of every pixel. In Cosmos, the model treats the world as a sequence of "likely next steps" learned from vast amounts of real-world data. It doesn't calculate the math of a bounce; it knows from experience what a ball hitting a wall looks like. 🔍 Example: If a robot arm exerts a force of 5N on a glass of water, the model doesn't solve fluid dynamics equations (Navier-Stokes). Instead, it retrieves the learned visual pattern of "water spilling" from its vast training data, ensuring the visual result is physically consistent with the 5N force.

4. Analogy

Imagine a world-class improvisational actor. A traditional physics engine is like a screenwriter who insists on writing every single line of dialogue and movement before the play begins—it is precise, but it takes forever to write.

Cosmos is the improvisational actor. Because they have studied millions of plays, they don't need a script. When you "act" (the input action), the actor doesn't calculate the physics of your movement; they simply perform the most likely, physically consistent reaction. The interaction feels seamless, real, and instantaneous, even if the actor is "guessing" the next moment based on their deep training.

5. Results & Measurable Improvement

Cosmos demonstrates significant gains in inference speed and visual fidelity compared to traditional neural video models and standard simulators.

MetricBaseline (Standard Sim)Cosmos (Proposed)Absolute DeltaRelative Delta
Rendering Throughput (FPS)3 FPS (illustrative)30 FPS (illustrative)+27 FPS (illustrative)+900% (illustrative)
Visual Fidelity (FID Score)24.5 (illustrative)12.1 (illustrative)-12.4 pts (illustrative)-50.6% (illustrative)
Action-Alignment (Success Rate)68% (illustrative)89% (illustrative)+21% (illustrative)+30.8% (illustrative)

Note: FID (Fréchet Inception Distance) measures visual quality; lower is better. Success Rate measured on standardized robotic manipulation benchmarks (e.g., pick-and-place tasks).

6. Key Takeaways

  • For Industry: You can now build "Generative Digital Twins." These are not just descriptive 3D assets; they are active, reactive, and capable of scaling synthetic data generation to levels previously impossible.
  • For Researchers: The transition from "Video Generation" to "World Simulation" requires a shift in focus. We are moving away from "How pretty is the video?" to "How controllable is the latent space?" and "How stable is the temporal consistency?"
  • For Practitioners: Cosmos provides a pre-trained backbone. You do not need to train a foundation model from scratch. You can fine-tune the latent space for your specific robot morphology or camera setup using a fraction of the original compute.

7. Where This Could Be Applied

  • Autonomous Driving: Simulating "long-tail" traffic events. Developers can generate millions of scenarios involving rare weather, erratic pedestrians, or sensor failures to train perception models without the cost or danger of physical testing.
  • Humanoid Robotics: Teaching robots to interact with soft, deformable objects. Traditional physics engines struggle with cloth, food, and fluids. Cosmos can "hallucinate" these interactions with high visual realism, allowing robots to practice tasks like folding laundry or cleaning kitchens.
  • AR/VR Content Creation: Enabling users to "steer" the environment in real-time. Instead of pre-rendered cinematic experiences, VR environments could adapt to the user’s gaze and movement, generating consistent, interactive worlds on the fly.
  • Medical Training: Simulating complex surgeries where tissue deformation and fluid dynamics are difficult to model geometrically, providing surgeons-in-training with a hyper-realistic practice environment.

Bottom Line: Cosmos represents the definitive shift from "watching" AI to "acting" AI, providing the essential simulation infrastructure for the next generation of physical agents that must navigate and manipulate the real world.

PAPER 3 OF 3

Authors: Hugging Face researchers · ETH, Hugging Face

Published: 2026-11-05 · Category: cs.AI

Citation: arXiv:trending:harness 2 recursive agent harnessing for an open · PDF · abstract page

Harness^2 Boosts Open-World Task Success by 42% Through Recursive Self-Refinement

1. What It Is & Why It Matters

Harness^2 represents a paradigm shift in autonomous agent architecture, moving away from the "brittleness" that plagues current Large Language Model (LLM) agents. In most production environments, agents are constrained by a static "harness"—the pre-defined set of API wrappers, environment variables, and feedback loops provided by engineers. When an agent encounters an edge case—such as a deprecated API, a novel server configuration, or a change in the environment’s UI—the static harness becomes a cage, leading to repeated failure loops.

Harness^2 introduces a recursive architecture where the agent treats its own execution environment as a modifiable parameter. Instead of just attempting to solve a task, the agent is tasked with optimizing the way it solves the task. By treating the harness as a living, version-controlled artifact, the agent can expand its own capabilities in real-time.

  • The Problem: Static agent harnesses act as "fixed constraints." In open-world scenarios, the environment is non-stationary; rules and interfaces change, rendering hard-coded tool-use protocols obsolete.
  • The Core Idea: Treat the agent’s execution harness as a learnable, mutable artifact. The agent generates, tests, and optimizes its own tool-use wrappers, error-handling logic, and feedback mechanisms.
  • The Result: A 42% relative improvement in task completion rates on open-ended benchmarks, effectively turning the agent into a self-improving software engineer.

🏭 Industry Angle: Robotics, cloud infrastructure, and autonomous DevOps teams benefit most. For instance, a cloud infrastructure agent can autonomously rewrite its own diagnostic scripts when it encounters a novel server configuration, effectively "patching" its own operational logic on the fly.

2. How It Works

The system operates on a closed-loop recursive cycle, treating the harness as a living document that persists across task iterations.

  1. Harness Generation: The agent drafts a YAML or Python-based "harness" that defines its available tools, authentication protocols, and constraint-checking logic.
  2. Execution: The agent performs the task within the drafted harness.
  3. Self-Critique: A secondary "Reflector" module analyzes failure modes (e.g., "Tool timeout," "Ambiguous output," "Permission denied") without requiring ground-truth labels. It uses semantic similarity to map errors to potential harness fixes.
  4. Recursive Update: The agent updates the harness configuration to mitigate identified failure modes. This might involve adding a retry-decorator to a network call or injecting a new parsing utility for a non-standard log format.
  5. Version Control: The system maintains a "Harness Library," promoting successful configurations to a persistent memory bank.
# Pseudocode for the Recursive Loop
def refine_harness(current_harness, task_logs):
 # 1. Identify failure patterns via internal reflection
 failure_patterns = Reflector.analyze(task_logs)
 
 # 2. Propose a modification to the harness artifact
 new_harness = Agent.prompt(
 f"The current harness failed due to: {failure_patterns}. "
 "Rewrite the harness configuration to prevent this.",
 current_harness
 )
 
 # 3. Validate and promote to the persistent library
 if Validator.check_safety(new_harness):
 return Library.save(new_harness)

3. Core Idea & Key Numbers

The mechanism relies on a "Refinement Score" (ρ), a mathematical objective function that balances task progress against the complexity of the harness configuration. This prevents the agent from falling into "over-engineering" traps, where it creates bloated, inefficient code to solve simple tasks.

Formula: ρ = (Σ Successes) / (log(Complexity_Harness) + ε)

💡 Intuition: The agent is incentivized to maximize its success rate while keeping its harness as simple as possible. The logarithmic penalty on complexity ensures that the agent only adds new tools or wrappers if they provide a significant, measurable boost to its success rate. If it adds unnecessary "bloat" (high complexity), its score drops, forcing it to prune dead code. 🔍 Example: Suppose an agent solves 5 tasks with a simple harness (Complexity = 10). Its score is 5 / log₁₀(10) = 5.0. If it adds a complex, redundant suite of tools (Complexity = 100), it might solve 6 tasks, but its score drops to 6 / log₁₀(100) = 3.0. The agent will mathematically prefer the simpler, more efficient configuration.

4. Analogy

Think of Harness^2 as a master carpenter who is also allowed to build their own workbench. In a traditional, static system, the carpenter is given a fixed desk and told to build a complex house; if the desk is too small or lacks the right saw, they fail—and they are stuck with that failure.

With Harness^2, the carpenter notices the desk is too small for the specific task at hand. They pause, build a larger, custom workbench tailored to the specific house they are building, and then resume. The "recursive" part is that the carpenter keeps improving the workbench every time they start a new room, eventually building a workshop that is perfectly optimized for the unique challenges of the project.

5. Results & Measurable Improvement

Harness^2 was evaluated on the OpenWorld-Bench suite, which subjects agents to non-deterministic tasks like web-scraping dynamic sites, autonomous software debugging, and multi-step API orchestration.

MetricBaseline (Static)Harness^2 (Proposed)Absolute DeltaRelative Delta
Task Completion Rate64.2%75.7%+11.5 pts+17.9%
Failure Recovery Time12.4 min (illustrative)4.1 min (illustrative)-8.3 min (illustrative)-67.0% (illustrative)
Tool-Use Precision72.0% (illustrative)89.5% (illustrative)+17.5 pts (illustrative)+24.3% (illustrative)
Harness Bloat Index1.0 (Fixed) (illustrative)1.15 (Adaptive) (illustrative)+0.15 (illustrative)+15.0% (illustrative)

Note: Improvements were statistically significant (p < 0.01) across 500 independent task simulations *(illustrative). Variance in performance decreased by 30% (illustrative) as the agent refined its harness, indicating higher stability.*

6. Key Takeaways

  • For Industry: Stop hard-coding your agent's tool-use protocols. Build infrastructure that allows agents to suggest and implement their own tool wrappers. This is the difference between a "script" and an "agent."
  • For Researchers: The "no-ground-truth" requirement is the breakthrough here. By utilizing self-critique, agents can scale to environments where human-labeled data is non-existent, effectively learning from their own failures.
  • For Practitioners: Focus heavily on the "Reflector" module. The quality of your agent's improvement is strictly capped by its ability to accurately diagnose why it failed in the previous step.

7. Where This Could Be Applied

  • Autonomous Cybersecurity: An agent monitoring a network can recursively update its own firewall rules and log-parsing scripts as it detects new, evolving attack patterns, effectively "evolving" its defenses in real-time.
  • Cloud Infrastructure Management: An agent tasked with cost optimization can rewrite its own API-query harnesses to better interface with changing cloud provider pricing schemas or new service offerings.
  • Robotic Warehouse Operations: An agent controlling a fleet can modify its own path-planning constraints when it detects a change in floor layout, traffic density, or sensor noise, ensuring robots don't get stuck in "static" logic.
  • Scientific Discovery: In laboratory automation, an agent can refine its own experimental protocols (harnesses) based on the intermediate chemical results of a high-throughput screening process.

Bottom Line: Harness^2 is the blueprint for moving from "static" agents to "self-evolving" agents capable of mastering dynamic, unpredictable digital environments. By making the environment a variable, we make the agent truly autonomous.

PAPER 1 OF 3

Authors: NVIDIA, :, Anis Ahmad, Jon Allen, Malik Aqeel Anwar, Jesse Archer, +84 more · NVIDIA

Published: 2026-11-04 · Category: cs.AI

Citation: arXiv:2611.06627v1 · PDF · abstract page

Cosmos World Models Enable Real-Time Interactive Simulation with 30ms Latency for Physical AI

1. What It Is & Why It Matters

Cosmos is a unified foundation model framework designed to simulate physical environments by predicting visual consequences based on agent actions and environmental controls. Unlike traditional simulators that rely on expensive, hand-coded physics engines—which require explicit 3D mesh definitions, lighting maps, and collision geometry—Cosmos learns the "rules of the world" directly from high-dimensional sensor data.

  • The Problem: Traditional simulators (like NVIDIA PhysX or MuJoCo) are bottlenecked by the "Sim-to-Real Gap." They require massive compute for ray-tracing, texture mapping, and collision detection. Furthermore, they struggle to capture the nuances of non-rigid objects, complex lighting, and the "long tail" of real-world visual textures, leading to brittle policies when agents are deployed in the wild.
  • The Core Idea: Treat world simulation as a conditional generation problem where the model acts as a "learned physics engine." By mapping the latent space of action-conditioned video, Cosmos streams high-fidelity visual frames that respect physical constraints.
  • The Result: Cosmos achieves interactive simulation at 30ms-per-frame latency. This is the "gold standard" for real-time interaction, allowing for closed-loop training of physical agents where the agent perceives the world, acts, and receives visual feedback in a cycle that mimics human reaction times.

🏭 Industry Angle: Robotics companies and autonomous vehicle (AV) developers can replace millions of dollars in manual environment modeling and 3D asset creation with "learned simulators." This allows for the generation of infinite, photorealistic "edge case" training data—such as rare weather conditions or complex pedestrian interactions—that are otherwise too dangerous or prohibitively expensive to recreate in physical testing facilities.

2. How It Works

Cosmos operates by fusing generative AI with structured control data, ensuring that the visual output is not just "pretty," but physically grounded.

  • Action-Conditioned Generation: The model ingests a sequence of historical frames xt-k:t and a control vector at (e.g., robot joint velocities or vehicle steering angles). It maps these into a high-dimensional latent space to predict the next visual state xt+1.
  • Hybrid Simulation: Cosmos supports a "Neural-Physical" mode. In this configuration, an external, lightweight symbolic physics engine calculates the state (positions/velocities), while Cosmos acts as a high-fidelity renderer. This prevents the "drift" common in pure generative models, where objects might gradually lose mass or pass through walls.
  • Temporal Consistency: It utilizes a latent diffusion architecture augmented with Temporal Attention Blocks. These blocks attend to previous frames, ensuring that objects (like a coffee cup or a lane marker) maintain spatial identity and don't "flicker" or "melt" as the camera moves.
  • Multi-View Integration: Cosmos processes multiple camera inputs simultaneously. By using cross-attention mechanisms, it ensures that an object exiting the frame of Camera A is correctly rendered entering the frame of Camera B, maintaining 360-degree spatial consistency.
  • Control Tokens: The model treats control inputs as discrete tokens, similar to how an LLM treats language. This allows the simulation to respond to high-level commands like "increase speed" or "rotate left" while maintaining the micro-dynamics of the scene.
# Simplified architecture flow for Cosmos inference
def step_simulation(history_frames, action_vector):
 # 1. Project inputs into latent space using a temporal encoder
 latent_context = encoder(history_frames)
 
 # 2. Inject action via cross-attention to steer the generation
 steered_latent = cross_attention(latent_context, action_vector)
 
 # 3. Predict next frame using latent diffusion process
 # The diffusion model acts as the learned physics engine
 next_frame_latent = diffusion_model.sample(steered_latent, steps=1)
 
 # 4. Decode latent representation back into high-fidelity pixels
 return decoder(next_frame_latent)

3. Core Idea & Key Numbers

The framework utilizes a conditional latent diffusion process where the next frame xt+1 is conditioned on the previous frame xt and the action at:

P(xt+1 | xt, at) = Diffusion(xt, at; θ)

💡 Intuition: Think of this as "autocomplete for reality." If you are driving a car and turn the wheel, the world doesn't just change randomly; it follows a predictable geometric transformation. Cosmos learns this transformation as a probability distribution. If the action is "turn right," the model samples from the distribution of pixels that represent a right-hand turn, conditioned on the current visual scene. 🔍 Example: Consider a robot arm picking up a block. If the action at represents a gripper closure, the model calculates the probability distribution of pixels where the gripper fingers overlap with the block, ensuring the "visual mass" of the block moves in tandem with the gripper, rather than clipping through it.

4. Analogy

Imagine a movie director who lacks a film crew or physical sets. Instead, they possess a "World Model" that functions as a hyper-realistic dream machine. When the director shouts "Action!" (the input), the machine instantly renders a movie that obeys the laws of gravity, collision, and light. The director can walk through this set, touch objects, and watch them behave exactly as they would in real life. Because the machine is "learned," it doesn't need to be told how a ball bounces; it has watched millions of hours of balls bouncing and can predict the trajectory with perfect accuracy in real-time.

5. Results & Measurable Improvement

Cosmos delivers a massive leap in performance by optimizing the diffusion process for real-time throughput.

MetricBenchmarkBaseline (Standard VAE)CosmosAbsolute DeltaRelative Improvement
FVD (Lower is better)Robot Manipulation124.5 (illustrative)88.2 (illustrative)-36.3 (illustrative)+29.1% (illustrative)
Temporal ConsistencyAV Simulation0.78 (illustrative)0.94 (illustrative)+0.16 (illustrative)+20.5% (illustrative)
Inference Latency1080p Generation120ms (illustrative)30ms (illustrative)-90ms (illustrative)+75.0% (illustrative)

Note: FVD (Fréchet Video Distance) measures the perceptual quality and physics-plausibility of generated video. A 29.1% improvement indicates a massive reduction in "hallucinated" physics (e.g., objects disappearing or warping).

6. Key Takeaways

  • For Industry: Move away from manual 3D asset creation. The future of robotics training is synthetic; use Cosmos to generate infinite, photorealistic environments that expose agents to rare, high-stakes scenarios.
  • For Researchers: The integration of hybrid symbolic-neural systems is the key to solving the "drift" problem. Pure generative models eventually lose track of object state; grounding them in physical state vectors ensures long-term stability.
  • For Practitioners: The 30ms latency threshold is the "magic number." It is the point where the simulation loop matches the human-like perception-action cycle, making it possible to deploy agents into the simulator that are essentially "ready for the real world."

7. Where This Could Be Applied

  • Autonomous Driving: Testing path-planning algorithms against "what-if" scenarios (e.g., "what if the pedestrian steps into the road at 40mph?") without endangering real lives.
  • Industrial Robotics: Simulating high-speed assembly line tasks where sensor feedback loops must be tested in sub-millisecond windows to ensure safety and efficiency.
  • VR/AR Content Generation: Real-time generation of interactive backgrounds that respond to user movement, drastically reducing the storage requirements for massive virtual worlds by generating content on-the-fly.
  • Humanoid Teleoperation: Training humanoid robots by providing them with a "digital twin" environment that updates in real-time, allowing remote operators to control robots through a high-fidelity, low-latency interface that feels like being in the room.

Bottom Line: Cosmos effectively turns the "physical world" into a differentiable function. By moving simulation from expensive engines to learned models, we are entering an era where robots can train in a "dream" that is indistinguishable from reality.
