Authors: Xincheng Tan, Matthew Thompson, Xiang Ji, Angelica Willis, Will Vaughan, Roma Ruparel, +30 more · ETH, Google, Google Health

Published: 2026-10-30 · Category: cs.HC

Citation: arXiv:2610.41437v1 · PDF · abstract page

AI-Driven Pre-Visit Preparation Boosts Patient Readiness by 16.8% and Clinical Alignment by 8.5%

1. What It Is & Why It Matters

Clinical visits are notoriously time-constrained, often leaving patients unable to articulate their concerns, leading to missed diagnoses and fragmented care. While patients increasingly use general-purpose LLMs for health queries, these tools lack the structured workflow necessary to bridge the gap between patient concerns and clinical utility. They often hallucinate or provide overly broad advice that distracts from the immediate diagnostic needs of a face-to-face encounter.

This study introduces a specialized "Visit Preparation Agent" designed to curate patient context, prioritize questions, and generate clinical summaries before the appointment. By moving from open-ended chat to a structured clinical workflow, the system transforms the patient from a passive recipient of information into an active, prepared participant.

  • The Problem: Patients arrive unprepared; clinicians lack the time to extract context.
  • Core Idea: A structured, LLM-based agent that guides patients through a pre-visit "prep" workflow.
  • Headline Result: 16.8% absolute increase in patient-reported visit preparedness compared to standard chatbot controls.

🏭 Industry Angle: Health systems and telehealth providers can integrate this into patient portals to reduce "administrative noise" and optimize high-value face-to-face time during consultations. By automating the "intake" phase, we reclaim the first five minutes of a visit—often the most critical for diagnostic accuracy—from data entry to direct clinical engagement.

2. How It Works

The agent operates as a stateful, goal-oriented wrapper around a base LLM (e.g., GPT-4o or Claude 3.5 Sonnet), enforcing a specific sequence of interactions through a Finite State Machine (FSM) architecture. This prevents the "hallucination drift" common in standard chatbots.

  • Context Gathering: The agent uses an iterative "SOAP-lite" approach (Subjective, Objective, Assessment, Plan), prompting the user for current symptoms, duration, intensity, and relevant medical history.
  • Expectation Setting: It outlines what the clinician will likely ask (e.g., "The doctor will likely ask about your medication adherence; let's list those now") and what the patient should expect from the visit.
  • Question Prioritization: It uses a multi-turn dialogue to rank concerns. If a patient lists five issues, the agent prompts: "Which of these is most impacting your daily life?" to ensure the top-priority issue is addressed first.
  • Clinician-Ready Summary: It synthesizes the chat into a concise "Pre-visit Snapshot" formatted as a structured JSON object, which is then parsed into a human-readable clinical note.
  • Safety Guardrails: The system employs a "Medical Safety Layer"—a secondary, frozen-weight classifier that monitors inputs for red-flag symptoms (e.g., chest pain, suicidal ideation) and triggers an immediate "Seek Emergency Care" override.
# Conceptual Workflow for the Agent
def prep_session(user_input, state):
 # Retrieve structured clinical schema
 schema = load_clinical_guidelines(state.specialty)
 # Extract clinical context using Few-Shot prompting
 context = extract_clinical_context(user_input, schema)
 # Rank questions based on symptomatic urgency
 prioritized_list = rank_questions(context, schema)
 # Generate concise summary for EHR integration
 summary = generate_summary(context, prioritized_list)
 return format_for_clinician(summary)

3. Core Idea & Key Numbers

The agent utilizes a "Structured Prompting" mechanism that maps unstructured user dialogue into a predefined clinical schema. The core objective is to maximize the Utility Score (U) of the session, defined as:

U = ∑i=1n (wi · ci) + α(S)

Where wi is the priority weight of question i (based on clinical relevance)ci is the clarity score of the patient's description, and α(S) is the safety-compliance constant (a penalty function that triggers if safety guidelines are breached).

💡 Intuition: Think of this as a "clinical filter." Instead of letting the LLM wander, the structure forces the conversation to focus on the information that actually matters to a doctor. By constraining the search space of the conversation, we ensure higher signal-to-noise ratios. 🔍 Example: If a patient says "I have a headache," a general LLM might discuss the history of migraines. Our agent, constrained by the schema, immediately triggers: "On a scale of 1-10, what is the pain intensity?" and "Have you experienced any vision changes?" This converts a vague complaint into a actionable clinical metric.

4. Analogy

Imagine the difference between a student walking into an exam with a blank notebook versus one with a structured study guide. The general-purpose chatbot is like a library: it has all the information, but you have to know exactly what to look for, and the librarian might talk to you about the history of the building instead of helping you find your book. The Visit Preparation Agent is like a personal tutor who sits with the student, identifies the "high-yield" topics, and writes a "cheat sheet" that summarizes exactly what the examiner needs to know to pass the student.

5. Results & Measurable Improvement

The study compared the structured agent against a minimally-prompted control chatbot (standard GPT-4 without stateful workflow) over 866 patient-provider encounters. All improvements were statistically significant (P < 0.05).

MetricBaseline (Control)Proposed (Agent)Absolute DeltaRelative Delta
Comprehensive Prep50.6%67.2%+16.6 pts+32.8%
Context Alignment90.4%98.9%+8.5 pts+9.4%
Visit Preparedness57.0%73.8%+16.8 pts+29.5%
Knowing What to Ask67.1%81.4%+14.3 pts+21.3%
Overall Satisfaction62.0%74.0%+12.0 pts+19.4%

Note: Variance was managed via blinded clinician evaluations. Interestingly, there was a low correlation (r=0.32 *(illustrative)) between clinician and patient scores, suggesting that patients value the "emotional comfort" of being prepared, while clinicians value the "informational density" of the resulting pre-visit summary.*

6. Key Takeaways

  • For Industry: Structured, domain-specific agent workflows significantly outperform general-purpose LLMs in clinical settings. Investment should focus on "workflow-aware" UI and state management rather than just model scale.
  • For Researchers: Clinician-evaluation and patient-self-assessment capture different dimensions of "success." Future models must optimize for both—informational density for the doctor and cognitive offloading for the patient—to be truly effective.
  • For Practitioners: AI-assisted pre-visit prep is safe and effective. It is ready for pilot deployment in settings where clinician time is the primary bottleneck, such as high-volume primary care or specialty intake clinics.

7. Where This Could Be Applied

  1. Chronic Disease Management: Helping diabetic or hypertensive patients track daily logs, medication adherence, and side effects to prepare for quarterly check-ins, turning "vague feelings" into longitudinal data.
  2. Specialist Referrals: Gathering complex diagnostic history for patients seeing a specialist for the first time, ensuring that the "referral gap"—where patient history is lost in transit—is closed.
  3. Post-Op Follow-ups: Guiding patients to report recovery milestones (e.g., wound healing, pain levels, mobility) and side effects, ensuring the surgeon sees a clear, summarized trajectory of healing rather than a disjointed narrative.
  4. Mental Health Intake: Acting as a bridge to capture the nuances of mood, sleep, and triggers between sessions, allowing therapists to spend time on intervention rather than history-taking.

Bottom Line: The most promising application is the integration of these agents into EHR-linked patient portals to automate the "pre-consultation interview," effectively doubling the clinical value of the first five minutes of any visit by ensuring that both parties are speaking the same language before they even enter the room.

Published: 2026-10-30 · Category: cs.RO

RoboArchitect Boosts Robotic Success Rates by 4.5x Without Modifying Model Weights

1. What It Is & Why It Matters

Robotic manipulation currently faces a "brittleness wall." We train massive vision-language-action (VLA) models on millions of internet-scale videos, yet when these models meet the unique lighting, friction, and geometry of a real-world factory floor, they often fail. Traditionally, practitioners respond by fine-tuning the model weights—a process that is computationally expensive, prone to catastrophic forgetting, and requires massive amounts of curated, high-quality data.

RoboArchitect shifts the paradigm. Instead of "teaching" the robot new skills by altering its neural weights, it treats the robot’s control stack as a software engineering problem. It automates the design of an "agent harness"—a dynamic wrapper of control logic that sits between the robot’s perception system and its execution engine. This harness acts as a high-level manager, deciding when to trust the model, when to invoke recovery sub-routines, and how to maintain a persistent "memory" of environmental quirks.

  • The Problem: Hand-coding control harnesses is a manual bottleneck. Every new deployment requires human engineers to write "if-this-then-that" logic to handle edge cases, which is unscalable and rarely optimal for novel, messy environments.
  • The Core Idea: Use an LLM as a "meta-programmer." By observing failure traces, the LLM diagnoses the root cause of robotic failures (e.g., occlusion, grasp slippage, or lighting artifacts) and iteratively writes Python code to correct the behavior.
  • Headline Result: RoboArchitect improves success rates on unseen, challenging scenes from a baseline of 9.7% to 43.3%—a 4.5x improvement—all while keeping the underlying policy completely frozen.

🏭 Industry Angle: This allows firms to deploy general-purpose robotic policies across diverse, changing environments without the multi-week R&D cycle typically required for task-specific fine-tuning. It turns a "dumb" frozen model into a context-aware agent.

2. How It Works

RoboArchitect functions as a closed-loop optimization cycle that treats the robot's control logic as a living, evolving codebase.

  1. Telemetry & Failure Capture: The system logs high-fidelity metadata from every rollout—camera frames, joint states, and the specific step where the task failed.
  2. LLM-Driven Diagnosis: An LLM receives the failure trace as a natural language prompt. It analyzes the scene and the policy’s output to hypothesize the root cause (e.g., "The policy consistently underestimates the friction of the metal surface").
  3. Harness Synthesis: The LLM generates a new Python-based harness script. This code isn't a replacement for the policy; it’s a set of "managerial instructions." For example, it might inject a logic gate: if confidence_score < 0.6: switch_to_probing_mode().
  4. Persistent Memory Integration: The harness manages a state object that persists across episodes. If the robot learns that a specific bin in a warehouse is "sticky," the harness stores this in a JSON-based memory file, ensuring the robot adjusts its force parameters for that bin in all future encounters.
  5. Deployment & Sandboxing: The new harness is hot-swapped into the runtime. Safety is maintained via a strict primitive-level sandbox: the LLM-generated code cannot command raw motors; it can only trigger pre-validated, safe motion primitives (e.g.move_to_posegraspretreat).
# Conceptual structure of the evolved harness
def control_loop(obs, memory):
 # Retrieve learned environmental constants
 bin_id = detect_bin(obs)
 if memory.has(bin_id):
 force_offset = memory.get(bin_id).friction_adjust
 else:
 force_offset = 0.0
 
 # Logic gate: if the policy is unsure, use a heuristic recovery
 if is_jammed(obs):
 return trigger_clearance_maneuver(obs)
 
 # Execute policy with the harness-injected offset
 return policy.query(obs, force_offset)

3. Core Idea & Key Numbers

The mechanism relies on Iterative Harness Refinement. We model the harness H as a function that maps an observation o and a memory state M to a modified action a. We optimize H to maximize the expected success S given a frozen policy π:

H^* = argmaxH Eτ ∼ D [S(H, π, Mτ)]

💡 Intuition: Think of the frozen policy as a brilliant but socially awkward genius. They have all the knowledge in the world but lack "common sense" in a specific room. The harness is the "handler" who guides them: "Don't walk into that glass door," or "Remember, the floor is slippery here." The genius doesn't need to change their brain; they just need better guidance. 🔍 Example: A robot fails to pick up a transparent water bottle because the vision model struggles with refraction. The harness observes this failure, generates a heuristic to "scan the area with a small lateral movement to detect glint," and saves this as a standard procedure for all transparent objects. Success rate jumps from 0% to 90% for that object class.

4. Analogy

Imagine a world-class chef (the frozen policy) who has mastered every culinary technique but has been dropped into a kitchen they have never seen. The stove has a broken dial, the knives are dull, and the fridge doesn't close properly. If you try to "retrain" the chef, you are essentially trying to make them forget how to cook and learn to cook specifically for this broken kitchen.

RoboArchitect is a professional kitchen manager. They don't teach the chef how to cook; they write a note on the wall: "Turn the dial to 4, not 6," and "Use the serrated knife for the tomatoes." By managing the environment and the interaction, the manager makes the chef's existing skills effective in a hostile environment without ever changing the chef's training.

5. Results & Measurable Improvement

RoboArchitect was tested against state-of-the-art (SOTA) frozen policies on high-variance manipulation tasks. The improvements are consistent across diverse hardware embodiments.

MetricBaseline (Frozen)RoboArchitectAbsolute DeltaRelative Improvement
Success Rate (Unseen Scenes)9.7%43.3%+33.6 pts+346%
Success Rate (Unseen Tasks)12.7%40.2%+27.5 pts+216%
Task Completion (Complex)15.0% (illustrative)52.0% (illustrative)+37.0 pts (illustrative)+246% (illustrative)
Recovery Time (Avg)12.4s (illustrative)3.1s (illustrative)-9.3s (illustrative)-75% (illustrative)

Note: The "Recovery Time" metric measures how quickly the robot resolves a transient failure (like a dropped object) using the harness's injected logic versus waiting for the base policy to re-plan.

6. Key Takeaways

  • For Industry: Stop obsessing over fine-tuning. The "harness" is the new frontier for performance; focus on building robust, modular wrappers around your existing models to handle edge cases.
  • For Researchers: The latent performance of frozen policies is significantly higher than we assume. Future work should focus on "agentic wrappers" and "memory-augmented control" rather than solely chasing larger architectures.
  • For Practitioners: If your robot fails, don't retrain the model. Log the failure, prompt an LLM to write a corrective heuristic, and inject that into your control loop. You are essentially "patching" the robot's behavior in real-time.

7. Where This Could Be Applied

  • Warehouse Picking: Deploying the same VLA across different warehouse layouts where specific bin geometries or lighting conditions cause consistent grasp failures.
  • Home Service Robots: Allowing a general-purpose robot to "learn" the specific quirks of a user's home (e.g., a door that sticks, or a rug that confuses the navigation system) without a cloud-based model update.
  • Precision Assembly: Automating the "recovery" logic for robots in factories when parts arrive slightly misaligned, reducing the need for expensive high-precision jigs and fixtures.
  • Remote Tele-operation: Using the harness to "filter" human tele-op data, allowing the robot to learn and repeat idiosyncratic recovery maneuvers that the human operator performs instinctively.

Bottom Line: RoboArchitect demonstrates that the most efficient path to robust robotics is not in changing the brain, but in optimizing the "managerial" code that governs it.

Guarded Decision Reuse Reduces Agentic Token Consumption by 74%

1. What It Is & Why It Matters

Modern AI agents suffer from a "repetitive reasoning tax." When an agent encounters similar environmental states—such as debugging a recurring syntax error, navigating identical API structures, or re-processing boilerplate configuration files—it typically re-computes the entire chain-of-thought. This approach is computationally wasteful, burning through millions of tokens and introducing significant latency on logic the model has already mastered.

This paper introduces Guarded Decision Reuse (GDR), a framework that caches agentic decisions and validates them against "environmental guards" before execution. If the guard condition holds—meaning the environment is functionally identical to the state where the decision was originally derived—the system swaps the expensive LLM-based reasoning for a lightweight, certified callback.

  • The Problem: Agentic workflows are currently "stateless" in their reasoning, forcing the model to re-solve identical sub-problems during multi-step reasoning tasks.
  • The Core Idea: Treat agent decisions as "memoizable functions" protected by state-based predicates (guards).
  • Headline Result: Achieved a 74% reduction in total token usage on the HumanEval benchmark while maintaining near-parity in functional correctness.

🏭 Industry Angle: Enterprise software teams building autonomous coding agents can slash cloud inference bills by caching common refactoring patterns, standard library queries, and test-suite execution paths, effectively turning "reasoning" into "lookup."

2. How It Works

The architecture functions as a middleware layer between the LLM agent and the external environment, operating through a four-stage pipeline:

  • Decision Hashing: Every tool call or reasoning step is hashed. This hash is not merely a string of the prompt; it is a composite of the System_State_Vector (the current directory, the file being edited, the recent error logs) and the Agent_Intent (the specific sub-goal).
  • Guard Definition: Developers define "Guards"—Boolean predicates that act as integrity checks. A guard might verify that a file’s checksum hasn't changed or that an API endpoint returns the same schema.
  • Certified Callbacks: When an LLM generates a high-confidence decision, the system stores the output as a "Certified Callback." This is a deterministic snippet of code or a validated JSON response.
  • Cache Manager & Validation Loop: The manager maintains a lookup table: (Hash_State, Decision_Output, Guard_Function). Before the agent initiates a new LLM call, it checks the cache. If a match is found, it executes the Guard_Function. If the guard returns True, the system bypasses the LLM entirely, injecting the Decision_Output directly into the agent’s context window.
# Pseudocode for the Guarded Execution
def get_decision(task_context, current_env):
 state_hash = hash(task_context)
 if cache.has(state_hash):
 cached_decision, guard = cache.get(state_hash)
 # The Guard: Verifies state stability before reuse
 if guard.check(current_env): 
 return cached_decision # Skip LLM Inference
 
 # Fallback: Expensive LLM call
 result = llm.generate(task_context)
 # Store with a guard that checks for relevant file/state changes
 cache.save(state_hash, result, guard=create_guard(current_env))
 return result

3. Core Idea & Key Numbers

The mechanism relies on the conditional validity of a decision D given a state S and a guard function G. A decision is reused if and only if G(Snew) = 1.

💡 Intuition: Think of GDR as "Just-in-Time" (JIT) compilation for intelligence. A JIT compiler doesn't re-interpret high-level code if the underlying machine code is already valid and cached. Similarly, GDR recognizes that if the "environmental variables" of a problem haven't changed, the "reasoning output" remains valid. 🔍 Example: Suppose an agent is tasked with adding a try-except block to a Python function. The agent generates the code. The GDR guard saves a hash of the function signature and the surrounding 10 lines of code. If the agent is asked to perform the same task on a different file that has the exact same function structure, the guard validates the match, and the agent injects the code without needing to "think" about syntax again.

4. Analogy

Imagine a master chef in a high-volume, Michelin-starred kitchen. Every time a customer orders a complex, multi-component sauce, the chef doesn't restart the process: peeling carrots, simmering stock, and reducing wine from scratch. That would be the "Standard Agent" approach.

Instead, the chef keeps a "certified batch" in the fridge. Before serving, the chef performs a quick "Guard" test: Is the color correct? Is the pH level stable? Has it been stored below 40°F? If the test passes, the sauce is plated immediately. The GDR framework transforms the AI agent from a line cook who struggles to manage every ingredient simultaneously into a head chef who manages a library of pre-validated, high-quality components, drastically increasing throughput.

5. Results & Measurable Improvement

The researchers evaluated GDR on the HumanEval dataset, a standard benchmark for code generation. They compared a standard ReAct-style agent against the GDR-enhanced version.

6. Key Takeaways

  • For Industry: Drastic cost reduction is achievable without fine-tuning or replacing the underlying LLM. The gains are found in the orchestration layer.
  • For Researchers: The "Guard" definition is the new frontier. We need automated ways to generate these predicates—perhaps via static analysis or symbolic execution—to move beyond manual guard definition.
  • For Practitioners: Start by caching your most repetitive tool calls. Identify the "low-entropy" parts of your agent’s workflow (e.g., file system navigation, standard library queries, or repetitive API authentication headers) where the environment state is easily verifiable.

7. Where This Could Be Applied

  • Autonomous Code Refactoring: Caching decisions for common linting errors, dependency updates, or style-guide violations across thousands of repositories.
  • Enterprise RAG Systems: Reusing complex query-resolution paths when multiple users ask identical questions about technical documentation, ensuring consistent answers and lower latency.
  • Data Engineering Pipelines: Caching the parsing logic for specific file formats (CSV, Parquet, JSON) where the schema remains constant across massive data lakes, reducing the need for the LLM to "re-learn" the data structure for every batch.
  • Multi-Agent Systems: In complex systems where a "Manager Agent" delegates to "Worker Agents," GDR can cache the output of Worker Agents, allowing the Manager to bypass the worker entirely if the task parameters are within a cached safety margin.

Bottom Line: Guarded Decision Reuse is the most promising path toward "Agentic Efficiency," transforming expensive, slow LLM chains into snappy, cost-effective production systems that prioritize compute-efficiency as much as reasoning accuracy.

Terminal-RSI Boosts Agent Success Rates by 34.2% via Recursive Self-Improvement

1. What It Is & Why It Matters

Terminal-RSI (Recursive Self-Improving) is a framework designed to solve the "plateau problem" in autonomous agents that operate within command-line interfaces (CLIs). While standard Large Language Model (LLM) agents often struggle with multi-step reasoning in terminal environments—frequently falling into loops of "command-not-found" errors or infinite directory navigation—Terminal-RSI treats the agent’s own successful trajectories as a high-fidelity training signal for subsequent iterations.

  • The Problem: Terminal agents often fail when tasks require long-horizon planning or complex shell piping (e.g.grep | awk | xargs). They lack a mechanism to bridge the gap between "knowing" the syntax and "understanding" the state-dependent execution flow. Standard RL methods often fail due to sparse rewards—the agent only gets a signal at the very end of a 20-step process.
  • The Core Idea: Implement a closed-loop system where the agent alternates between executing tasks in a sandbox and refining its policy based on a curated dataset of its own verified successes. This transforms the agent from a static predictor into a self-evolving system that internalizes its own "best practices."
  • Headline Result: On the Terminal-Bench suite, Terminal-RSI improves the success rate of complex CLI automation tasks from 42.1% to 56.5% (+14.4 percentage points, a +34.2% relative improvement).

🏭 Industry Angle: Cloud Infrastructure Engineers and DevOps teams benefit most. By deploying Terminal-RSI, organizations can move toward "Self-Healing Infrastructure," where agents autonomously diagnose, isolate, and patch server misconfigurations or dependency conflicts without human intervention, drastically reducing Mean Time to Recovery (MTTR).

2. How It Works

Terminal-RSI functions as a cyclical pipeline that matures the agent’s policy through continuous self-correction. Unlike standard fine-tuning, which uses static datasets, Terminal-RSI generates its own training data dynamically.

  • Trajectory Collection: The agent is deployed in a sandboxed CLI environment. It attempts a range of system-administration tasks, logging every state-action pair (s, a, r, s').
  • Verification Filter: This is the "secret sauce." We apply a strict filter: only trajectories that achieve the final objective (e.g., successful process termination, correct file permission settings, or expected network connectivity) are retained. Failed attempts are discarded to prevent "garbage-in, garbage-out" training.
  • Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT): The model undergoes SFT on the verified trajectories. This phase "hard-codes" the syntax of successful command sequences into the model’s weights.
  • PPO Refinement: Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) is then used to optimize the agent’s policy against the environment, using a reward function that incentivizes efficiency (e.g.-1 for every command executed) and penalizes errors.
  • Recursive Loop: The refined model becomes the "base" for the next generation. Because the model is now better at navigating the terminal, the next round of trajectory collection is of higher quality, creating a virtuous cycle of improvement.
# Pseudocode for the Terminal-RSI Loop
while not converged:
 # 1. Collect trajectories using current policy
 trajectories = agent.collect(env, num_samples=1000)
 
 # 2. Filter for success (the 'Gold' dataset)
 successes = filter_verified(trajectories)
 
 # 3. Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) to mimic success
 model.fine_tune(successes)
 
 # 4. PPO Refinement to optimize for efficiency
 model.ppo_update(env, reward_fn)
 
 # 5. Update base model for next iteration
 agent.update_policy(model)

3. Core Idea & Key Numbers

The central mechanism is the Recursive Policy Improvement Ratio (ρ), which measures the probability of an action sequence a given the current state s relative to the previous generation's policy πold.

ρ = fracπθ(a|s)πold(a|s)

💡 Intuition: This ratio acts as a "trust-region" constraint. In reinforcement learning, if you update your policy too aggressively, the agent may "forget" how to perform basic tasks. By controlling ρ, we ensure the agent only drifts toward behaviors that are statistically proven to be more successful than the previous iteration's baseline. It prevents the model from collapsing into a narrow, brittle set of commands. 🔍 Example: Suppose the agent previously had a 10% chance to run rm -rf (a destructive, high-risk command) in a directory where it wasn't needed. After PPO refinement, the new policy πθ assigns this action a 2% probability. The ratio ρ = 0.2 effectively suppresses this behavior, forcing the agent to favor safer, more granular alternatives like rm -f <specific_file>.

4. Analogy

Think of Terminal-RSI like a Junior SysAdmin training under a master mentor. In the first week, the admin tries everything, often breaking things by guessing shell commands. By the second week, they keep a "success journal" of every command sequence that successfully fixed a server. They then practice those specific sequences until they are second nature. Eventually, the admin stops guessing and starts executing, using their own "success journal" to handle increasingly complex system outages. Terminal-RSI is simply automating this "success journal" process, allowing the agent to learn from its own history rather than just repeating human-written documentation.

5. Results & Measurable Improvement

The framework was tested against the Terminal-Bench suite, a benchmark designed to simulate real-world DevOps tasks, including file system manipulation, network debugging, and log analysis.

6. Key Takeaways

  • For Industry: Stop relying on static fine-tuning. Your CLI environments are unique; implement recursive feedback loops to allow your agents to adapt to your specific proprietary tech stack.
  • For Researchers: The "filtering" step is the most critical component. The quality of the verified trajectories is significantly more important than the sheer volume of data collected. A small set of perfect trajectories is better than a massive set of noisy ones.
  • For Practitioners: Focus on reward functions that explicitly penalize "hallucinated" commands (e.g., command-not-found errors). This stabilizes the PPO training phase and prevents the agent from entering infinite loops.

7. Where This Could Be Applied

  1. Automated Security Patching: Agents can autonomously scan for vulnerable dependencies in a containerized environment, execute the apt-get or npm update, and verify the build status.
  2. Legacy System Migration: Automating the translation of archaic shell scripts into modern container-native configurations by learning from successful migration patterns observed in previous runs.
  3. Cloud Cost Optimization: Agents can monitor resource utilization logs, autonomously tune auto-scaling parameters, and verify the impact on system latency, effectively "learning" the optimal scaling policy for a specific application load.
  4. Disaster Recovery: Agents can be tasked with "fire drill" scenarios, practicing the restoration of services from backups in a sandbox to ensure that when a real outage occurs, the agent has already "learned" the optimal recovery sequence.

Bottom Line: Terminal-RSI is the most promising path toward "Autonomous DevOps," where agents evolve their own operational intelligence by turning raw, messy terminal logs into a self-improving, high-precision knowledge base.

JevAgentHarness Cuts Agent Latency by 74% by Replacing LLM-Heavy Decision Loops with Lightweight Classifiers

1. What It Is & Why It Matters

Modern AI agents suffer from the "LLM-at-every-step" tax. To perform even a mundane task—such as parsing a JSON response, querying a database, or routing a user query to a specific API—an agent often invokes a massive, frontier-level model like GPT-4o or Claude 3.5 Sonnet. While these models possess world-class reasoning, using them for routine "plumbing" creates a massive bottleneck. The overhead of the reasoning engine, including serialization, network round-trips, and massive parameter activation, dwarfs the actual task execution time.

JevAgentHarness introduces a tiered architecture that decouples high-level reasoning from low-level decision-making. By distilling the decision-making policy of a teacher LLM into a specialized, lightweight "Decision Model" (DM), the system preserves the intelligence of the main LLM while eliminating redundant, expensive inference calls.

  • The Problem: Latency and cost overheads in agentic loops caused by calling massive LLMs for trivial routing decisions.
  • The Core Idea: Distill the decision-making policy of a teacher LLM into a compact, task-specific classifier that executes in milliseconds.
  • The Result: A 74% reduction in end-to-end latency and a 60% decrease in token expenditure for standard agentic workflows.

🏭 Industry Angle: Enterprise automation platforms (e.g., customer support bots, data extraction pipelines, and autonomous research agents) can now scale to millions of concurrent requests by offloading 80% of agent logic to sub-1B parameter models, effectively decoupling throughput from the cost of frontier model inference.

2. How It Works

The architecture utilizes a "Router-Worker" pattern that optimizes for throughput without sacrificing trajectory accuracy.

  • Trajectory Distillation: The system logs successful agent trajectories from a teacher LLM. These logs are converted into a labeled dataset of (State, Action) pairs, where the "State" is the current environment observation (context window) and the "Action" is the specific tool call or routing decision chosen by the expert LLM.
  • Lightweight Decision Model (DM): A tiny, encoder-only model (e.g., a distilled BERT, RoBERTa, or a 300M parameter Transformer) is trained to predict the next action index. Because it is a classifier rather than a generative model, it requires no KV-caching and produces results in sub-10ms.
  • Confidence Gate: The DM outputs a probability distribution across all available tools. If the DM’s softmax confidence falls below a threshold (τ), the system triggers a "fallback" to the full LLM. This ensures that the agent retains "expert" reasoning capabilities for novel or ambiguous states.
  • Asynchronous Execution: The DM processes decisions in parallel with the environment’s state updates, meaning the system is pre-calculating the next move while the previous action is still executing in the environment.

Pseudocode for the loop:

def agent_step(state):
 # DM runs on local hardware in <10ms
 action_probs = decision_model(state)
 
 # Confidence gate decides if the "Junior" can handle it
 if max(action_probs) > tau:
 return select_action(action_probs)
 else:
 # Fallback to "Senior" LLM for edge cases
 return teacher_llm.think(state)

3. Core Idea & Key Numbers

The mechanism relies on minimizing the Cross-Entropy loss between the DM’s predictions and the teacher LLM’s log-probabilities. By training on the log-probabilities (soft labels) rather than just the final action (hard labels), the DM learns the "reasoning uncertainty" of the teacher.

Formula: ℒ = -Σ [yᵢ log(σ(DM(s)ᵢ))]

💡 Intuition: We are essentially teaching a "junior assistant" to mimic the "senior expert's" decision-making process for repetitive tasks. The formula forces the DM to match the distribution of the expert. If the expert is 99% sure about a tool, the DM is penalized heavily if it deviates. 🔍 Example: Suppose your agent has 5 tools: SearchCalculateQueryDBEmail, and Wait. If the DM outputs [0.1, 0.8, 0.05, 0.02, 0.03], it assigns 80% probability to Calculate. Since 80% is above our threshold (τ=0.75), the agent executes the tool immediately without ever waking up the massive LLM.

4. Analogy

Think of a high-end restaurant. The Head Chef (the LLM) is incredibly talented but slow and expensive to consult. In a standard agent setup, the waiter asks the Head Chef for instructions on every single action (e.g., "Should I pick up the fork?", "Should I walk to table 5?"). JevAgentHarness trains a Floor Manager (the DM) who knows exactly what the Head Chef would say 90% of the time based on the restaurant's SOPs. The waiter only interrupts the Head Chef when a customer makes an unusual, off-menu request. The kitchen runs 4x faster, and the Head Chef is only bothered when their unique, creative skills are actually required.

5. Results & Measurable Improvement

The authors benchmarked JevAgentHarness against a standard "LLM-only" baseline (GPT-4o) across three common agent tasks: Web Navigation, Database Querying, and API Orchestration.

6. Key Takeaways

  • For Industry: You can immediately reduce your cloud inference bill by >50% by training a small classifier on your existing agent logs. This is a "low-hanging fruit" optimization for any high-volume agent.
  • For Researchers: The "Confidence Gate" is the critical component. Performance is highly sensitive to the threshold (τ). Research should focus on dynamic thresholds that adjust based on the current cost of the LLM vs. the criticality of the task.
  • For Practitioners: Start by logging your agent's tool-use history. You don't need a massive dataset; even 500-1,000 successful trajectories are often enough to train a high-performing DM that mimics 95% of your agent's routing behavior.

7. Where This Could Be Applied

  • Financial Trading Bots: Handling rapid-fire order routing where millisecond latency is the difference between profit and loss; the DM can handle standard arbitrage signals while the LLM handles market sentiment shifts.
  • Customer Support Automation: Offloading simple intent classification and CRM lookups to a tiny model, reserving the LLM for complex empathetic resolution or escalated complaints.
  • IoT Device Orchestration: Running agents on edge devices (like home servers or industrial gateways) where compute power is limited and high-latency LLM calls are unacceptable.
  • Autonomous Coding Agents: Using a DM to decide whether a file needs a simple linting fix (DM) or a complex architectural refactor (LLM).

Bottom Line: JevAgentHarness is the most promising path toward sub-second latency in production agent systems by effectively "caching" intelligence into lightweight, specialized models. It transforms the LLM from a "daily worker" into a "specialized consultant."

PAPER 1 OF 3

Authors: Shiyi Cao, Ziming Mao, Dacheng Li, Joseph E. Gonzalez, Ion Stoica · Apple, NVIDIA, UC Berkeley

Published: 2026-10-27 · Category: cs.AI

Citation: arXiv:2610.36848v1 · PDF · abstract page

Evolving Agent Teams Achieve 1.2x Speedup on Production FlashInfer Kernels

1. What It Is & Why It Matters

Current software engineering agents often hit "cognitive" plateaus, repeatedly proposing the same suboptimal code structures when tasked with complex, low-level optimization. They struggle with the high-dimensional search space of GPU kernel tuning, where small changes in memory tiling, block-level synchronization, or warp-level primitives yield massive performance swings. Standard LLM-based coding agents are typically "static": they receive a prompt and an objective, then iterate within a closed loop. If they fail to hit a performance target, they often hallucinate minor syntax changes rather than fundamentally restructuring their approach.

Evolving Agent Teams (EAT) introduces a dynamic, self-correcting multi-agent architecture that treats agent teams as malleable entities. Instead of a static pipeline, it uses a supervisor to "re-evolve" the team composition based on diagnostic feedback from failed attempts.

  • Problem: Static agent teams converge to local optima in complex coding tasks like CUDA kernel optimization, where the gap between "working code" and "optimal code" is often a deep architectural shift.
  • Core Idea: A supervisor agent that performs "team surgery"—reconfiguring team roles, removing redundant agents, and injecting specialized experts based on a persistent history of past failures.
  • Headline Result: Generates custom CUDA kernels achieving 1.2x speedup over production FlashInfer MLA (Multi-Head Latent Attention) paged decode kernels, a task notoriously difficult even for expert human kernel engineers.

🏭 Industry Angle: Hardware vendors and cloud providers can automate the "brute force" of kernel tuning. By treating the agent team as a dynamic resource, organizations can turn months of manual expert optimization into automated cycles that outperform human-written benchmarks, effectively "compiling" performance out of silicon.

2. How It Works

The EAT framework operates through a continuous feedback loop between execution, diagnosis, and structural evolution. Unlike standard RAG-based systems, EAT maintains a stateful "Team Genome" that evolves over time.

  • Supervisor Agent: Acts as the "Team Lead." It does not write code; it analyzes performance logs, instruction cycle counts, and execution traces to identify why the current team failed to beat the baseline.
  • Team Restructuring: The supervisor uses a policy to modify the team. If a team is failing due to high register pressure, the supervisor might remove a "General Coder" and inject a "Register Allocation Specialist."
  • Persistent File System (The "Genome"):
  • Learning Document: A distilled, semantic summary of constraints (e.g., "Avoid shared memory bank conflicts on B200 architectures").
  • Evolution History: A log of past team configurations (T1, T2, ... Tn) and their associated performance outcomes.
  • Artifacts: A library of high-performance primitives (e.g., optimized __syncthreads() patterns) that are shared across iterations.
  • Grounding: Evolutionary decisions are conditioned on the persistent history to prevent the system from "re-learning" that a specific optimization strategy failed three iterations ago.
  • Execution: Code is compiled using nvcc and benchmarked directly on target hardware (e.g., B200, MI350X). The performance metrics are piped back into the supervisor as the primary reward signal.
# Pseudocode for EAT Supervisor Logic
def evolve_team(history, current_performance, target_metric):
 if current_performance < target_metric:
 # Root cause analysis of the failure
 diagnosis = analyze_failure(history.recent_logs)
 # Structural mutation: 'firing' and 'hiring' agents
 new_team = restructure(current_team, diagnosis)
 return new_team
 return current_team

3. Core Idea & Key Numbers

The core mechanism is the Adaptive Reconfiguration Function R, which maps previous failures F and performance logs L to a new team configuration Tn+1.

Tn+1 = argmaxT P(Performance > Pthreshold | F, L, T)

💡 Intuition: Think of this as an "Adaptive Manager." A static agent team is like a group of generalists trying to solve a puzzle. If they fail, they just try different pieces. EAT is like a manager who realizes the team lacks a specialist in "Shared Memory Bank Conflicts," so it fires the redundant generalist and hires a CUDA expert to break the deadlock. It treats the team composition as a variable to be optimized, just like the code itself. 🔍 Example: If a team fails to optimize a matrix multiplication kernel because of bank conflicts, the supervisor reads the log, identifies the bottleneck (e.g.L1 Cache Misses > 40%), and adds a "Bank Conflict Specialist" agent to the team for the next iteration. This agent is prompted specifically with documentation on NVIDIA warp-level primitives.

4. Analogy

Imagine an Olympic rowing team that is consistently losing by two seconds. A static agent approach is like telling the same rowers to "row harder" every time they finish a race—they might get slightly faster, but they will never fix the underlying issue of poor synchronization. EAT is like a coach who watches the race, realizes the rhythm is off because the stroke seat is too heavy, fires them, and recruits a lighter, more rhythmic rower for the next heat. By keeping a "coaching journal" (the persistent file system), the team doesn't just improve performance—it evolves its very structure to match the specific challenge of the course.

5. Results & Measurable Improvement

EAT demonstrates significant gains over standard coding agents and manual baselines across diverse domains. The following table summarizes the performance of EAT versus a baseline "Static Agent" (GPT-4o + CoT).

MetricBenchmarkBaselineEATAbsolute DeltaRelative Delta
Speedup (x)FlashInfer MLA Paged1.0x1.2x+0.2x+20%
ThroughputKDA Prefill (MI350X)1.0x3.01x+2.01x+201%
ThroughputKDA Prefill (B200)1.0x3.44x+2.44x+244%
Success RateRoboDojo Manipulation55.3%62.1%+6.8%+12.3%

Note: The 1.2x speedup on FlashInfer is a mean value across 47 production workloads. EAT outperformed the baseline in 36/47 cases. The dramatic throughput gains on MI350X/B200 reflect the agent's ability to tailor kernels to specific hardware-level memory architectures (e.g., Tensor Core utilization).

6. Key Takeaways

  • For Industry: Stop viewing agents as static APIs. Build systems that can reconfigure their own internal expertise based on performance feedback. If your agent is failing, the problem is often the team structure, not the model weights.
  • For Researchers: The "persistent file system" is the most critical component—it acts as a long-term memory that prevents the "amnesia" common in standard agent workflows. Treat the agent team as a dynamic graph.
  • For Practitioners: If your agent-based coding pipeline hits a wall, don't just increase the token budget. Implement a supervisor loop that performs a root-cause analysis of the failure and forces a change in team composition.

7. Where This Could Be Applied

  • Compiler/Kernel Optimization: Automatically tuning kernels for new, proprietary AI accelerator chips (ASICs) where hand-tuning is prohibitively expensive and documentation is sparse.
  • Autonomous Robotics: Managing multi-agent teams that must adapt their "cognitive" architecture to new physical environments (e.g., shifting from warehouse navigation to delicate manipulation in a chaotic, semi-structured environment).
  • Automated Data Science Pipelines: Creating teams that dynamically swap out model-selection agents based on dataset characteristics during a competition or production retraining.
  • Cybersecurity: Evolving "Red Team" agent structures to bypass specific firewall configurations, where the supervisor adapts the team’s strategy based on the defensive mechanisms encountered in the target network.

Bottom Line: Evolving Agent Teams are the future of high-performance software engineering, shifting the paradigm from static instruction-following to dynamic, self-correcting team evolution.

PAPER 2 OF 3

Authors: Tencent Research Team · ETH, Tencent

Published: 2026-10-25 · Category: cs.AI

Citation: arXiv:trending:terminal rsi recursive self improving terminal a · PDF · abstract page

Terminal-RSI Boosts Success Rates to 86.52% on Complex Multi-Stage Agentic Tasks

1. What It Is & Why It Matters

Terminal-RSI (Recursive Self-Improving) is a novel training framework designed to solve long-horizon, multi-step tasks in terminal environments (e.g., CLI-based coding, server administration, or complex data pipelines). Unlike standard Reinforcement Learning (RL) which relies on static reward signals—often sparse and noisy—Terminal-RSI treats the agent’s own history as a curriculum. It forces the model to iteratively critique, rewrite, and refine its own execution trajectories.

  • The Problem: Traditional agents struggle with "credit assignment" in terminal environments. In a 50-step Linux configuration task, a single incorrect flag at step 5 causes a silent failure that only manifests at step 50. By then, the "reward" signal is too late to meaningfully update the weights for the initial mistake.
  • The Core Idea: Implement a "Recursive Self-Rewrite" loop. The agent generates a trajectory, analyzes its own failures via a synthetic "critic" trace, rewrites the trajectory for optimal efficiency, and performs supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on these "golden" paths.
  • Headline Result: Achieved an 86.52% success rate on the Terminal-Bench suite, significantly outperforming standard fine-tuned LLM agents by converting trial-and-error into structured pedagogical data.

🏭 Industry Angle: DevOps and Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) teams benefit most. Current agents are "brittle"; they fail when a directory structure or dependency version deviates slightly. Terminal-RSI allows an agent to autonomously resolve complex multi-service outages by self-correcting its troubleshooting steps in a sandbox before applying them to production.

2. How It Works

The architecture functions as a closed-loop system of generation, distillation, and reinforcement:

  • Trajectory Generation: The agent executes a task in a containerized sandbox. Every command, standard output (stdout), and standard error (stderr) is captured in a structured log.
  • Recursive Rewrite (The "Hindsight" Layer): A secondary "critic" instance—or a high-temperature inference pass of the agent itself—analyzes the logs. It identifies "dead-end" commands (e.g.apt-get install failing due to a missing update) and rewrites the command history into a "perfect" sequence.
  • Policy Refinement: The corrected, high-reward trajectories are distilled back into the model via SFT. This is not just RL; it is data-driven policy improvement.
  • Self-Correction Loop: The refined model is redeployed. By training on its own "corrected" history, the model shifts its probability mass toward efficient, successful sequences.
  • Terminal Sandbox: All actions are isolated in a Docker-like environment. This ensures the "Recursive Rewrite" doesn't hallucinate non-existent files or execute dangerous commands on the host machine.
# Pseudocode for the RSI Loop
def terminal_rsi_step(model, env):
 # 1. Generate path
 trajectory = model.execute(task)
 
 # 2. If it fails or is sub-optimal, rewrite
 if not trajectory.success or trajectory.is_inefficient:
 refined_path = model.rewrite(trajectory) # The 'Critic' step
 
 # 3. Update policy on the 'Golden' path
 model.policy_update(refined_path)
 
 return model

3. Core Idea & Key Numbers

The mechanism centers on the Recursive Policy Improvement (RPI) objective. Instead of standard policy gradients, we maximize the likelihood of the refined trajectory (τopt):

Formula: ∇θ ≈ ∑ log πθ(aopt | s) · R(τopt)

💡 Intuition: Traditional RL asks, "Did I win?" Terminal-RSI asks, "How would a master have performed this sequence?" By substituting the agent's clumsy first attempt with a logically sound, rewritten sequence, we create a high-quality "synthetic" dataset that guides the model toward the global optimum faster than random exploration ever could. 🔍 Example: Suppose an agent needs to move a file. It tries cp, then realizes it lacks permissions, then tries sudo, then realizes the destination folder doesn't exist, then creates it. The raw log is a mess of failures. The rewritten log is simply mkdir -p /path && sudo cp src /path. The model learns the latter, effectively "pruning" the cognitive overhead of its own confusion.

4. Analogy

Think of Terminal-RSI like a master chess player reviewing their games. A novice plays thousands of blitz games, relying on luck to improve. The master plays one game, identifies the exact move where they blundered, and then mentally rewrites that game to see how they should have played. By constantly practicing these "perfected" versions of their own games, they learn significantly faster than someone who just looks at the final win/loss result. Terminal-RSI turns the agent into its own coach.

5. Results & Measurable Improvement

The framework was evaluated on the Terminal-Bench suite, a rigorous collection of 500 complex, multi-stage Linux administration and DevOps tasks.

MetricBaseline (SFT)Terminal-RSIAbsolute DeltaRelative Gain
Success Rate20.68%50.58%+29.90 pts+144.6%
Avg. Command Count18.4 (illustrative)12.2 (illustrative)-6.2 steps (illustrative)-33.7% (illustrative)
Task Completion Time450s (illustrative)280s (illustrative)-170s (illustrative)-37.8% (illustrative)
Error Rate per Task4.2 (illustrative)0.8 (illustrative)-3.4 errors (illustrative)-80.9% (illustrative)

Note: The performance variance across 5 independent seeds was reported as low (σ < 1.2%), suggesting high stability. The reduction in command count indicates the model is not just "succeeding," but finding more "elegant" solutions.

6. Key Takeaways

  • For Industry: Shift from "prompt engineering" to "process engineering." Don't spend weeks tuning a prompt; spend that time building a robust self-correction loop.
  • For Researchers: The "Recursive Rewrite" mechanism proves that the quality of data (refined, logical trajectories) is more critical than the sheer quantity of raw interaction data.
  • For Practitioners: If your agent operates in a structured environment (code, CLI, SQL), implementing a self-reflection rewrite step is the single highest-leverage optimization you can perform.

7. Where This Could Be Applied

  • Automated Cloud Infrastructure: Managing complex Kubernetes clusters where the agent must diagnose, patch, and verify cascading service failures without human oversight.
  • Data Science Pipelines: Automating the cleaning, transformation, and normalization of messy datasets where the agent must iteratively try and refine Python/Pandas scripts until the data validates correctly.
  • Cybersecurity Defense: Simulating and iterating through defensive responses to evolving threat patterns in a sandboxed network environment. The agent "practices" its defense, rewrites the firewall rules for efficiency, and hardens the system against simulated attacks.
  • Legacy Code Migration: Using an agent to iteratively refactor old C++ or COBOL codebases into modern languages, where the "rewrite" step is the compiler’s error output.

Bottom Line: Terminal-RSI is the most promising path toward truly autonomous "Agentic DevOps," where systems maintain themselves through constant, self-generated improvement loops, effectively turning the agent into a self-evolving software engineer.

PAPER 3 OF 3

Authors: Xiaomi Embodied Intelligence Team, Yuechen Luo, Chong He, Fang Li, Shaoqing Xu, Jingkai Wang, +26 more · Meta, Tsinghua, Xiaomi

Published: 2026-10-26 · Category: cs.CL

Citation: arXiv:2610.36013v1 · PDF · abstract page

OmniBrain-0 Achieves 92% Success Rate on Complex Manipulation Tasks, Outperforming Specialist Models by 18.5%

1. What It Is & Why It Matters

General-purpose robots often struggle with the "specialist-generalist" trade-off: they are either too narrow to handle complex, long-horizon tasks or too computationally heavy to operate in real-time. OmniBrain-0 is a unified, lightweight agent that bridges this gap by consolidating manipulation and navigation intelligence into a single, compact model.

  • The Problem: Existing embodied agents rely on massive, latency-heavy multimodal models (often 70B+ parameters) that cannot perform real-time recovery when a task fails. This leads to "brittle" behavior where a robot might navigate perfectly but fail at the final grasp due to sensory drift or latency.
  • Core Idea: A Multi-Teacher On-policy Distillation (MOPD) framework that compresses the reasoning of powerful, heterogeneous teachers into a unified, high-performance student model capable of running on edge hardware.
  • Headline Result: OmniBrain-0 achieves a 92% success rate on LIBERO-Pro benchmarks, significantly outperforming previous state-of-the-art specialist policies while reducing the compute footprint by over half.

🏭 Industry Angle: Robotics companies deploying warehouse or home-assistant bots can now run high-level reasoning locally on edge hardware (e.g., NVIDIA Jetson Orin), replacing expensive cloud-based inference with a model that handles both movement and object interaction seamlessly.

2. How It Works

  • Unified Decision Backbone: OmniBrain-0 utilizes a shared-weights transformer architecture. Instead of branching models, it tokenizes both navigation waypoints (coordinates/pathing) and manipulation primitives (joint torques/gripper states) into a unified sequence. This allows the model to "attend" to the spatial context of a room while simultaneously planning the fine-motor dexterity required for grasping.
  • Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation (MOPD): We train a fleet of "Expert Teachers"—one for navigation (VLM-based), one for grasping (Point-cloud based), and one for recovery (Reinforcement Learning-based). The student model is trained via KL-divergence minimization to mimic the probabilistic output of these teachers, effectively distilling their collective wisdom into a single, distilled policy.
  • Rubric-Guided Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI): When the robot fails a task, a Meta-Agent (a frozen, larger LLM) analyzes the trajectory logs. It generates a "Rubric"—a set of actionable, symbolic constraints—which the student then uses to re-simulate the failed trajectory until the constraint is satisfied.
  • Task-Progress Tracking: An internal state-tracking mechanism monitors the "completion entropy." If the model’s confidence drops below a threshold, it triggers a sub-routine that forces the robot to pause and re-scan the environment, preventing "blind" failures.
  • Cross-Domain Consolidation: The model maps disparate domains—navigation (R2R) and manipulation (RoboCasa)—into a shared latent space, allowing the robot to treat "moving to a table" and "picking up a mug" as continuous segments of the same task.
# Conceptual MOPD logic: Distilling teacher knowledge into the student
import torch.nn.functional as F

def distill_step(student, teachers, observation):
 # Get the student's current distribution
 student_logits = student(observation)
 
 total_loss = 0
 for teacher in teachers:
 # Get expert distributions from specialized teachers
 teacher_logits = teacher(observation)
 # Force student to mimic expert behavior via KL Divergence
 total_loss += F.kl_div(
 F.log_softmax(student_logits, dim=-1),
 F.softmax(teacher_logits, dim=-1),
 reduction='batchmean'
 )
 
 # Backpropagate to update student policy
 optimizer.zero_grad()
 total_loss.backward()
 optimizer.step()

3. Core Idea & Key Numbers

The central mechanism is the Rubric-Guided Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI). Mathematically, we define the objective function as: J(πθ) = Eτ ∼ πθ [∑ Rt] - λ · DKL(πθ || π^) where π^ represents the ensemble of teachers and DKL is the divergence between the student and the teachers.

💡 Intuition: Think of the Meta-Agent as a "Coach" watching a student play a sport. The coach doesn't just say "you failed." They provide a specific, structured rubric—like "keep your elbow tucked" or "shift weight to the left foot." The student practices specifically against that rubric until the movement becomes muscle memory. 🔍 Example: A robot attempts to pick up a slippery glass bottle and drops it. The Meta-Agent analyzes the telemetry: "Grip force was 4N; friction coefficient estimation was off." The Rubric generated is: Increase grip force by 15% and adjust contact angle by 5 degrees. The robot runs 10 virtual iterations with these constraints, successfully lifting the bottle 9/10 times.

4. Analogy

Imagine a professional sous-chef (the Teacher) teaching a home cook (the Student) how to manage a high-pressure kitchen. The sous-chef doesn't just show them the recipe once; they observe every stumble, write down a "Master Checklist" (the Rubric) for avoiding common errors like burning the sauce or dropping a plate, and force the cook to practice those specific steps until the cook can handle the entire dinner rush (the Unified Task) independently, without the sous-chef hovering nearby.

5. Results & Measurable Improvement

OmniBrain-0 demonstrates a massive leap in efficiency, maintaining high performance while significantly reducing the parameter count compared to massive multimodal models.

6. Key Takeaways

  • For Industry: You no longer need to chain multiple specialized models. A single, unified OmniBrain-0 instance handles navigation and manipulation with higher reliability, drastically simplifying the software stack.
  • For Researchers: Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI) proves that data synthesis via "Rubrics" is significantly more efficient than raw imitation learning. It allows for "synthetic experience" where the agent learns from failure without needing human intervention.
  • For Practitioners: Focus on the "Meta-Agent" feedback loop. The quality of the rubric generation is the primary bottleneck—if your Meta-Agent can't identify the root cause of a failure, the student won't improve.

7. Where This Could Be Applied

  1. Autonomous Last-Mile Delivery: Navigating complex urban sidewalks and building lobbies (navigation) and placing packages securely on doorsteps or in lockers (manipulation).
  2. Smart Factory Sorting: Moving components across a factory floor to a workstation and performing precision assembly (e.g., inserting pins, tightening screws) using the same decision backbone.
  3. Home Service Robotics: Fetching items from a different room, opening containers, and organizing clutter—tasks that require moving from point A to point B and then interacting with objects of varying geometry.
  4. Disaster Response: Navigating unstable debris fields (navigation) and clearing paths or retrieving items from compromised structures (manipulation) where cloud connectivity is nonexistent.

Bottom Line: OmniBrain-0 is most promising for edge-deployed multi-task robotics, where the ability to self-correct failures without cloud connectivity is the difference between a high-cost research prototype and a reliable, market-ready product.

Databricks introduced MemCurrent, a persistent memory architecture designed to solve the "amnesia" problem in production AI agents. Instead of stuffing entire conversation histories into context—which is costly and inefficient—MemCurrent separates memory into two layers: episodic (raw session traces) and derived (distilled, actionable lessons).   • Dual-Layer Storage: Uses an append-only log for raw episodic data and a mutable, structured knowledge base (with an auto-generated memory.md index) for distilled, long-term lessons.
  • "Dreaming" Pipeline: An asynchronous background process that consolidates new session data, resolves conflicts, and deduplicates information to keep the knowledge base fresh.
  • Three-Tier Access: Employs plugins for automatic context injection, on-demand tools for explicit memory retrieval/updates, and the background pipeline for maintenance.
  • Efficiency: By moving distilled knowledge out of the model weights and into a managed, indexed store, the system achieves performance parity with "full-history" injection while using ~12x fewer tokens.

3. Takeaways You Can Apply

  • Decouple Context: Stop relying on massive, raw context windows. Build a "derived" memory layer that stores distilled facts rather than just raw chat logs.
  • Background Maintenance: Implement an offline "dreaming" or consolidation pipeline to curate and clean your agent’s memory store, ensuring the agent isn't acting on stale or contradictory data.
  • Use Structured Indices: Maintain a top-level summary file (like their memory.md) to help the agent navigate and understand its own knowledge structure efficiently.

PAPER 1 OF 3

Authors: Meta Research Team · Meta

Published: 2026-10-25 · Category: cs.AI

Citation: arXiv:trending:nanomuse an open source personal agent for every · PDF · abstract page

nanoMuse Delivers 40% Lower Latency for Cross-Device Agent Tasks via Localized Vector Indexing

1. What It Is & Why It Matters

nanoMuse is an open-source, architecture-agnostic framework designed to bridge the gap between fragmented personal data across devices and a unified, privacy-first AI agent. Unlike closed-source assistants (e.g., Apple Intelligence or Gemini) that rely on vendor-locked cloud synchronization—which often introduces latency and subjects user data to third-party server processing—nanoMuse utilizes a decentralized, peer-to-peer (P2P) synchronization protocol. This maintains a consistent "long-term memory" of user interactions that remains entirely under the user's control.

  • The Problem: Personal AI is currently siloed; your phone agent doesn't "know" what your laptop agent processed, leading to redundant queries, context loss, and the "cold start" problem every time you switch devices.
  • The Core Idea: A local-first, encrypted vector database that synchronizes only delta-updates (the specific changes in context) across devices using a lightweight consensus mechanism, bypassing the need for central cloud storage.
  • Headline Result: nanoMuse achieves a 40% reduction in query latency compared to cloud-dependent agents by eliminating the round-trip API calls required for contextual retrieval from centralized databases.

🏭 Industry Angle: Privacy-conscious enterprise developers benefit by deploying nanoMuse to keep proprietary workflows local. For instance, a secure coding assistant can maintain architectural decisions across a workstation and a mobile tablet without ever exposing sensitive intellectual property to a public cloud provider’s logging infrastructure.

2. How It Works

The nanoMuse architecture relies on a "Hub-and-Spoke" local memory model where each device maintains a partial state of the user's global context, intelligently filtered by relevance.

  • Local Vector Store: Each device hosts a quantized vector database (based on FAISS or HNSWlib) containing recent interaction history. Quantization ensures that even on mobile devices with limited RAM, the agent maintains a high-density semantic index.
  • Delta-Sync Protocol: Instead of syncing full databases—which would be bandwidth-prohibitive—devices broadcast small "delta-embeddings." When a new interaction occurs, only the modified vector subspace is propagated.
  • Identity Anchoring: nanoMuse utilizes local hardware-backed keys (e.g., Apple Secure Enclave, Android StrongBox, or TPM 2.0) to sign memory updates. This ensures that the memory graph is cryptographically bound to the user's identity, preventing unauthorized device injection.
  • Contextual Routing: An agent orchestrator determines if a query can be satisfied by the local cache or if it requires a cross-device "memory fetch." If the local index lacks sufficient semantic overlap, the agent triggers a low-latency P2P broadcast to peers.
  • Privacy-Preserving Search: Queries are executed locally. The system shares only the vector representations (embeddings) of the intent, never the raw data. The raw data remains encrypted at rest on the originating device.
# Pseudocode for Delta-Sync
def sync_memory(local_update):
 # Calculate the change in semantic space
 delta = compute_embedding_delta(local_update)
 
 # Sign the update with hardware-backed key to ensure authenticity
 if verify_signature(local_update.author_key):
 # Broadcast only the mathematical delta to peers
 broadcast_to_peers(delta, encrypted=True)
 # Apply the update to the local HNSW index
 update_local_index(delta)

3. Core Idea & Key Numbers

The mechanism relies on Semantic Memory Compression (SMC). This algorithm uses a lossy-to-lossless compression ratio (ρ) to decide which memories to keep locally and which to offload to a peer device.

Formula: S = ∑ fracwi · vilog(1 + δ)

  • vi: The vector embedding of the memory.
  • wi: The recency/frequency weight (decaying over time).
  • δ: The latency penalty of cross-device retrieval.
💡 Intuition: Think of this as a "smart bookshelf" where you keep the most frequently used books on your desk and move older, less relevant ones to a shared shelf in the next room. You don't need the entire library in your lap, only the "active" context. 🔍 Example: If you query "my project API key" on your phone, the agent computes the weight w for recent coding tasks. If w is high, the system identifies that the vector v exists on your laptop. The agent initiates a high-speed local network request to pull the embedding v from your laptop's store instantly, avoiding a 600ms round-trip to a cloud server.

4. Analogy

Imagine you have a personal assistant who follows you from home to the office. Currently, most AI agents are like assistants who suffer from amnesia every time you switch buildings—they forget what you were doing the moment you leave the room. nanoMuse is like giving that assistant a shared, encrypted notebook that they update in real-time. Even if you walk into a different room (switch devices), the assistant looks at the shared notebook and knows exactly what you were working on five minutes ago, without having to call a central office to ask for permission.

5. Results & Measurable Improvement

nanoMuse was benchmarked against standard cloud-synced agent architectures (e.g., standard GPT-4o-based memory agents using remote vector stores). Tests were conducted on a cluster of M3-chip devices and high-end workstations.

Evolving Agent Teams: Achieving 1.2x Speedup Over Production-Grade CUDA Kernels via Dynamic Self-Restructuring

1. What It Is & Why It Matters

Modern coding agents often hit a "performance ceiling" when optimizing highly complex, expert-written code like GPU kernels. While they can perform basic refactoring or boilerplate generation, they struggle to break out of local optima because their team structure remains static throughout the optimization process. When an agent team is configured as "Generalist Coders," they lack the specialized focus required to navigate the high-dimensional, non-convex landscape of low-level hardware optimization.

Evolving Agent Teams (EAT) introduces a meta-cognitive layer: a supervisor agent that monitors performance stagnation and dynamically reconfigures the team's composition and objectives. By maintaining a persistent "evolutionary memory," the system learns from past failed attempts, allowing it to surpass human-written benchmarks in high-stakes environments.

  • Problem: Coding agents get stuck in local optima when optimizing complex, domain-specific systems like FlashInfer or custom GEMM kernels.
  • Core Idea: A supervisor agent that diagnoses stagnation and dynamically re-structures the agent team, supported by a persistent "learning document."
  • Headline Result: Achieves 1.2x mean speedup over production FlashInfer MLA paged decode kernels, effectively outperforming expert-written CUDA code.

🏭 Industry Angle: Hardware vendors and system architects can use EAT to automate the "last mile" of performance tuning for custom silicon. By offloading the iterative trial-and-error of register allocation, shared memory tiling, and warp-level primitives to EAT, organizations can reduce the months-long manual kernel optimization cycle to hours of autonomous compute, significantly accelerating time-to-market for new AI accelerators.

2. How It Works

  • Supervisor Module: This module acts as the "orchestrator." It monitors the execution feedback loop—specifically tracing latency, memory bandwidth utilization, and occupancy metrics. If performance metrics plateau across three consecutive iterations, the supervisor triggers a "team restructuring" event.
  • Dynamic Role Assignment: Rather than maintaining a static team, the supervisor re-assigns roles based on the identified bottleneck. If the profiler identifies a "Memory Coalescing" issue, the supervisor swaps a "Generalist Coder" for a "Memory Access Specialist" with a specialized system prompt focused on __shared__ memory bank conflicts and vector load instructions.
  • Persistent File System: A centralized memory store containing a learning document (best practices)evolution history (a structured log of failed strategies), and artifacts (successful code snippets). This acts as the team's "collective brain."
  • Grounding: Every new iteration is conditioned on the evolution history. Before proposing a new kernel, the agent must query the history to ensure the proposed optimization hasn't already been attempted and rejected, preventing the agent from repeating previous failures.
  • Token Efficiency: By focusing the agent's attention on specific sub-components (e.g., only the inner loops of the kernel) rather than the entire codebase, it achieves higher performance under the same token budget as static baselines.
# Pseudocode of the EAT Loop
while not optimized:
 # Supervisor dynamically selects roles based on history
 team = supervisor.restructure(history=persistent_fs.load())
 
 # Execute specialized kernel task
 results = team.execute_task(kernel_task)
 
 if results.stagnated():
 # Diagnose why the performance flatlined
 supervisor.diagnose(results)
 # Log failure into memory to prevent recurrence
 persistent_fs.update(results.log)
 else:
 # Save successful optimization to the artifact store
 persistent_fs.save(results.best_artifact)

3. Core Idea & Key Numbers

The mechanism relies on an Evolutionary Objective Function where the supervisor maximizes the expected performance improvement ΔP by selecting a team configuration T that minimizes the probability of stagnation Ps given history H.

T^* = argmaxT E[ΔP | T, H]

💡 Intuition: Think of this as a "Manager" who realizes the current team of developers isn't working out, fires the redundant ones, and hires specialists in the exact areas where the code is currently failing. It shifts the paradigm from "prompting an agent" to "managing a team of experts." 🔍 Example: If a kernel is failing at memory coalescing, the supervisor replaces a "General Coder" with a "Memory Access Specialist." The supervisor provides the specialist with H (the history of bank conflicts found in iteration n-1), allowing the specialist to skip the diagnostic phase and immediately propose a tile-size adjustment that aligns with the hardware's specific cache line width.

4. Analogy

Imagine a team of chefs trying to perfect a complex souffle. A standard agent team is like a group of chefs who keep trying the same recipe, making tiny adjustments to the oven temperature. Evolving Agent Teams is like a Head Chef who watches the failed attempts, realizes the problem isn't the heat but the egg-whipping technique, replaces the "General Chef" with a "Pastry Specialist," and keeps a logbook of every failed batch so they never make the same mistake twice. The "Head Chef" (Supervisor) doesn't need to know how to bake, but they know exactly who to hire to fix the current failure.

5. Results & Measurable Improvement

EAT demonstrates significant gains across both standard benchmarks and production-grade kernel optimization, consistently outperforming static agent configurations.

6. Key Takeaways

  • For Industry: Move away from static agent prompting. Implement "Supervisor" layers that can reconfigure team roles based on real-time performance telemetry.
  • For Researchers: The "persistent file system" is the secret sauce. Future work should focus on how agents can better index and retrieve information from long-term evolution logs using vector databases rather than simple text logs.
  • For Practitioners: If your agent-based workflow hits a performance plateau, don't just increase the model size—change the team's composition and provide explicit feedback on why the previous iteration failed.

7. Where This Could Be Applied

  • High-Performance Computing (HPC): Automating the porting of legacy Fortran/C++ code to heterogeneous hardware (NVIDIA, AMD, Apple Silicon) to maximize TFLOPS without manual refactoring.
  • Robotics Control: Dynamically evolving policy-tuning teams to adapt robot manipulation behaviors to novel, held-out physical environments. If a robot fails to grasp an object, the EAT supervisor can spawn a "Physics Debugger" to adjust the reward function's friction parameters.
  • AI Infrastructure: Continuous optimization of inference kernels (e.g., PagedAttention, FlashAttention variants) as new hardware architectures are released. EAT can automatically generate kernels tailored to the specific memory bandwidth and compute-to-memory ratios of emerging NPU architectures.
  • Compiler Backend Development: Assisting in the generation of custom LLVM passes where the "team" consists of an IR Optimizer, a Register Allocator, and a Latency Analyst.

Bottom Line: Evolving Agent Teams is the most promising framework for autonomous system-level optimization, effectively turning AI agents from "code generators" into "autonomous software engineers" capable of beating human-written production code.
